Acme Analytics — Customer Story Podcast Recording

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-12
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~42 minutes
Location: Zoom (recording)
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood), Ethan (Redwood), Priya (Redwood), Maya (Acme), Liam (Acme), Sofia (Acme)

Auto sections (lightly edited):
Summary: A conversational, semi-scripted podcast-style interview to capture Acme's experience migrating inference traffic to Redwood Dedicated and how that changed cost, latency, and developer productivity. Focus on two human stories: how the product marketing team launched a new feature faster, and how the platform team reduced per-request cost.
Topics covered: intro, business problem, technical approach, outcomes, quote capture, approvals process

Transcript body:
[00:00:00] Jordan Patel: All right we're recording, hey everyone, thanks for joining — this is Jordan from Redwood Marketing, we're doing the customer story podcast with Acme Analytics. Quick mic check, can you hear me OK?
[00:00:08] Maya Alvarez: Yeah loud and clear. Hi hi, excited.
[00:00:11] Liam O'Connell: Yep, good to go.
[00:00:13] Ethan Cole: Awesome. I'm Ethan, I'll be lightly guiding the conversation, won't hog it.
[00:00:20] Jordan: Cool. So the plan — we'll do about 30 minutes of recorded Q&A, capture a few short soundbites for the case study, then 10 minutes of notes and follow ups. Sound good?
[00:00:29] Maya: Sounds great. We're happy to share the story.

[00:00:33] Ethan: Great — Maya, maybe start us off with the high-level problem you were trying to solve before Redwood. Keep it informal, like you'd tell a customer.
[00:00:40] Maya: Sure. So uh Acme had been embedding LLM features into our search product, and the early stages were on hosted endpoints from other vendors, but when we moved into a real rollout we started seeing cost spikes and, erm, latencies that were inconsistent across regions. The marketing team needed predictable response times for the demo flows and we couldn't risk a slow demo in live customer meetings. Also there was a lot of concern around data residency and audit logs — like we needed to know where inference traffic was going.
[00:01:08] Ethan: And prior to Redwood you were running the models through third-party hosted APIs?
[00:01:12] Maya: Yeah, exactly — a mix of hosted providers, and some on-prem experiments. It worked for prototypes but not for scale.

[00:01:20] Jordan: Liam, as CTO, what pushed you toward Redwood Dedicated rather than fully self-hosting or staying hosted with big cloud vendors?
[00:01:28] Liam O'Connell: Good question. From an infra perspective, two things — control and predictability. We needed a way to guarantee a baseline throughput during big spikes — think Black Friday style volume for our customers — but we didn't want the ops burden of maintaining the whole stack ourselves. Redwood gave us reserved GPU pools and autoscaling configs that matched our traffic patterns, plus the routing/fallback features were attractive because we could keep a hosted fallback for non-critical workloads. Also the KV cache optimizations — small but it compounded.
[00:02:00] Jordan: When you say KV cache optimizations, can you put that into plain english for marketers listening?
[00:02:05] Liam: Uh yeah, basically we saw repeated prefixes during query patterns — like help center prompts — and Redwood's runtime could cache those internal token states, so subsequent requests were cheaper and faster, like fewer tokens to compute.
[00:02:18] Priya Rao: If I can add a note, there was also an improvement in tail latency because of continuous batching and better kernel selection on the hardware we used. The SLOs got much more predictable.

[00:02:30] Ethan: Great, that actually makes a nice soundbite — "predictable SLOs" — we'll mark that. Maya, tell us a concrete example of how this changed a launch timeline or campaign.
[00:02:39] Maya: Oh sure. We had a campaign for a new smart-replies feature. In the old flow we had to schedule model runs and had a two-week buffer for performance tuning because latency was a wild card. With Redwood Dedicated, the PM and engineering could iterate in days. We had the feature in a public beta in nine days from prototype — I think that was 60% faster than before, rough number.
[00:02:58] Jordan: Do you recall any numbers on cost change once you moved to Redwood? Even ballpark helps for marketing.
[00:03:03] Sofia Ramos: We did a 90-day comparison. Per-1000 inference cost dropped about 35% after we tuned batching and enabled quantized model variants for some non-critical endpoints. There was a bit of extra commitment cost for reserved capacity but overall unit economy improved. I can send that spreadsheet — anonymized.
[00:03:21] Ethan: Perfect, that's exactly the metric we want to quote with your approval.

[00:03:24] Maya: One thing I'd emphasize — the support from Redwood SEs during the PoC was key. Priya and team did a day of pairing to get performance graphs and prod-like load tests. That helped our PMs feel confident.
[00:03:36] Priya: Yeah we ran a canary style rollout and instrumented token-level cost metrics so they could see the impact in the console.

[00:03:42] Jordan: Let's switch to security and compliance — marketers like to reassure customers. Liam, any hurdles there and how did Redwood help?
[00:03:49] Liam: We had two big asks: SSO/SAML for team access and KMS integration for model keys / encryption. Redwood's Private offering meant we could run in a VPC with a customer-managed KMS, and they provided SOC 2 artefacts which fed our internal audit; that made procurement move quicker. There was a bit of back-and-forth on network egress rules but Redwood worked with our infra team.
[00:04:12] Maya: That was a relief. Our legal team wanted to avoid vendor lock-in language too and Redwood's contracts were reasonable.

[00:04:18] Ethan: Great — that's another good quote: "procurement moved quicker" — we'll mark.

[00:04:24] Jordan: A few quick lightning questions for soundbites: What surprised you most about working with Redwood? Sofia?
[00:04:31] Sofia Ramos: Honestly — the speed of iteration. I expected bandwidth friction when we switched infrastructure, but the opposite happened. Also, the quality monitoring tied to prompt sets saved us from a regression that would have hit our demo flows.
[00:04:44] Maya: For me, it's the cross-team visibility in the console — PMs could see latency breakdowns without pinging infra. That changed our daily standups.

[00:04:54] Jordan: Nice. Any concerns or things you'd caution other customers about? Real talk.
[00:05:00] Liam: Do expect some configuration work up front. If you have custom models or weird sequence lengths, you'll need to spend time on quantization choices and autoscaling curves. But that's par for the course.
[00:05:11] Maya: Also check on compliance needs early — that saved us time later.

[00:05:16] Ethan: OK couple of editorial questions — Maya, can you give a 1–2 sentence "hook" for the case study intro about the business impact?
[00:05:24] Maya: Yeah — "Acme Analytics cut model serving costs by over a third and accelerated feature launches by 60% after moving to Redwood Dedicated, enabling product marketing to ship demo-ready experiences faster." Does that sound ok?
[00:05:36] Jordan: That's excellent, we'll refine wording but that's a keeper.

[00:05:39] Priya: Minor note — let's not disclose exact customer counts or raw latency numbers without sign-off, we'll use averages or percent improvements.
[00:05:47] Sofia: Agreed. We'll produce anonymized numbers.

[00:05:50] Ethan: On approvals — what's the process and timeline for sign-off, Liam?
[00:05:54] Liam: To keep it fast, Maya owns marketing sign-off, I own technical sign-off for any metrics. Legal needs 48 hours for contract references; expect 5 business days max.

[00:06:06] Jordan: Noted. We'll send a draft and request approvals inline.

[00:06:10] Ethan: Recording housekeeping — any off-the-record comments?
[00:06:13] Maya: No, all good to record.

[00:06:16] Jordan: Cool. We'll capture a few more short anecdotes for audio. Maya, tell us about a customer story where a demo saved a deal because it didn't choke.
[00:06:25] Maya: There was a sales call where the demo previously timed out dealing with multi-turn prompts. We simply didn't show it — previously we'd pre-recorded. After Redwood's lower tail latency, the AE could demo live and the customer signed within a week. It's small but it's a strong narrative.

[00:06:44] Ethan: Nice. Short edit: "from pre-recorded demos to live demos that close deals" — good line.

[00:06:50] Jordan: We're at about 30 minutes of recorded content — let's plan the close. Any final comments or guardrails?
[00:06:57] Sofia: Please avoid mentioning the names of internal test accounts or our vendor partners in the public case study.
[00:07:03] Maya: And include the "developer velocity" angle. It matters for product marketing.

[00:07:08] Jordan: Got it. Last thing — logistics: We'll email the draft case study and a short list of quote snippets. We also might want 1–2 short audio clips from today's recording; will that be ok?
[00:07:18] Liam: Yes. Also, can Priya follow up with a one-page tech diagram? That would help our engineering blog team.
[00:07:25] Priya: Yep, I'll send that.

[00:07:28] Jordan: Perfect. Thanks everyone — we'll wrap the recording now. Off the record, quick 10 min sync for approvals and next steps.
[00:07:35] [Recording stopped — informal notes continue briefly]

[00:07:38] Jordan: (informal) Priya, remind me later about the kernel-selection graph we ran — I want one screenshot.
[00:07:45] Priya: Will do.

End of transcript.

Notes about transcript quality: informal, occasional word swaps (e.g., "KV cache" heard as "K V cache"), minor interruptions, some timestamps approximate.

OrionWorks runtime compatibility check-in

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-18
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Sophie Carter (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (OrionWorks, Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Platform Eng), Maya Chen (InfoSec)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy):
Customer evaluating migrating inference from a mixed stack (OpenAI hosted + on-prem vLLM/TGI) to Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private options. Key concerns: eval parity, latency, KV cache behavior, quantization effects, cost tradeoffs, security/KMS and SOC2 scope. Agreed to run POC benchmarking; Redwood to provide harness and pricing options.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sophie: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time, uh we'll do a quick intros then jump into what you're trying to accomplish. Aisha, do you want to kick us off with a little bit of context?
[00:09] Aisha: yeah sure. So, um OrionWorks we've been running customer-facing chat and document QA features. Right now it's a mix - we use OpenAI for a lot of high-quality generation, and we also have an on-prem inference fleet using vLLM/T-G-I stacks for lower cost, low latency in region stuff. The problem is parity and ops complexity, like two different runtime behaviours, uh and the teams want one place to run that gives consistent perf and ties to security controls.
[00:36] Marco: so you're running both OpenAI and a self-hosted vLLM/TGI? and are you doing quantization on the on-prem side?
[00:43] Tom: yeah, we quantize to 4-bit for most seq lengths; we use quantization for cost, but sometimes output quality degrades for few-shot prompts. Also kv cache management is custom - we have sticky sessions to keep cache warm for active users.
[00:58] Sophie: right, and what's the main driver for moving? Is it cost, reliability, compliance, or all of the above?
[01:05] Aisha: all of the above, but order of priority is: parity with OpenAI outputs for our customer-facing flows, then latency SLAs for live chat, and then cost predictability. Compliance is non-negotiable for some customers, so VPC or private deployment is on the table.
[01:21] Maya: from a security standpoint we need KMS/HSM integration, audit logs retained 13 months, and we're scoped for SOC2 in Q1. We also need to see encryption-in-transit details and SAML SSO for the console.
[01:33] Sophie: that's helpful. Redwood has three modes: Hosted API, Dedicated reserved pools, and Private (VPC/on-prem). For compliance we typically recommend Dedicated or Private. For the parity requirement you mentioned, we usually run eval parity tests which compare outputs and flag regressions. Can you describe the parity tests you run today?
[01:50] Aisha: we use a set of ~1200 prompts across intents, and we do automated similarity and human review on a subset. Our biggest worry is that when you switch kernels or quantize differently, the tokens change or there's higher hallucination, which then increases human review cost.
[02:07] Marco: yeah, quantization and kernel selection can change logits slightly; we can run the same prompt set and produce diff stats and confusion matrices. One question — are you using function-calls heavily or structured outputs?
[02:19] Tom: mostly structured JSON outputs for the QA system, yes function-calls for a subset, and streaming for chat.
[02:26] Sophie: perfect, that's useful. For streaming we support chunked responses and function-call semantics; for structured outputs we can pin sampler/temperature and provide reproducible seeds for evals.
[02:36] Aisha: how do you handle prefix/KV cache in Redwood? The vLLM stack we run has a pretty aggressive KV strategy that keeps prompts in memory per user session. If you move to hosted, will that kill our latency?
[02:48] Marco: good question. Our runtime supports automatic KV caching and also request-level sticky routing in Dedicated. In Hosted, we have a mix of caching layers — prefix cache and per-model KV cache — and we can align policies to mimic vLLM behavior. There are some latency tradeoffs if you can't have long-lived GPU-resident caches; Dedicated gives more control.
[03:05] Maya: is there a way to have customer-managed KMS in Hosted? we need KMS keys we control.
[03:10] Sophie: yes, for Private deployments you manage keys; for Dedicated we can integrate with customer KMS for disk and secret encryption; Hosted can support envelope encryption and bring-your-own-key in many cases, but we'll need to review specifics in the SOC doc. I'll attach the KMS section.
[03:23] Aisha: what's the typical performance delta between your Dedicated cluster and our vLLM current numbers? we see p99 latencies around 120ms for short prompts on our infra.
[03:32] Marco: depends on model and sequence length; for similar GPU type and quant profiles we typically match or beat VLLM for steady-state throughput due to our kernel selection and continuous batching. For cold-cache p99 we can be higher unless KV warm is available. We can run a direct benchmark.
[03:46] Tom: ok good. Another thing — we're on a custom TGI variant with some plugin ops. How much model-ops work is needed to onboard?
[03:54] Marco: usually we can onboard TGI models with minor adaptation; sometimes tokenizers or custom ops need small patches. We keep a compatibility map and we'll do a test run. If it's within common ops, we won't need deep changes.
[04:06] Sophie: timeline — do you have a hard date where you need to pick a path?
[04:09] Aisha: we'd like to run a POC before end of Q1; ideally kickoff in early Jan, have a 2–4 week POC with performance and parity checks, and then decide on Dedicated vs Private by mid-Feb.
[04:21] Sophie: that's doable. Proposal: two POC tracks — Hosted quick path (fast to start, lower friction) and Dedicated/Private track for parity and compliance. We'll scope both, you can pick which to run first.
[04:33] Maya: for procurement we will need standardized SOW and security questionnaire answered. Any enterprise paperwork ahead of POC?
[04:40] Sophie: we'll send a POC SOW and our security pack (SOC2, ISO references) and a short vendor questionnaire response. We'll also include sample SLAs for Dedicated.
[04:50] Marco: for the benchmark we'll want your target prompts, a representative batch distribution, and an example of your current vLLM config (quantization, batch sizes, tokenization). We'll run both throughput and quality evals and provide a parity report.
[05:02] Tom: can you share the harness? we'd rather run the baseline on our infra too.
[05:06] Marco: yes, we'll provide the harness; ideally we run Redwood-hosted baseline and you run the harness in your environment to compare apples-to-apples. We'll also instrument logs and trace tokens to help debug differences.
[05:17] Aisha: and pricing — what's the rough delta on cost for Dedicated POC vs Hosted?
[05:22] Sophie: quick ballpark: Hosted is usage-based, so POC can be lower entry; Dedicated has a small reserved footprint cost but predictable throughput which helps unit economics for high-volume. I'll include concrete numbers in the pricing sheet.
[05:34] Maya: one more security - we need attenuation on logs, redaction patterns for PII before logs leave our VPC. Is that something supported?
[05:41] Marco: yes, we support configurable redaction hooks and pre-send filtering in Private and Dedicated. For Hosted we have redaction rules but for regulated PII-heavy workloads we recommend Private so nothing leaves your control plane.
[05:55] Sophie: ok, looks like we have clear next steps. I'll send the SOW and security pack. Marco will drop the harness and run an initial run by Monday, 12/22. Maya will share the compliance contacts. Aisha will provide the prompt set.
[06:10] Aisha: great, thanks. Anything else?
[06:13] Tom: no, that's it from infra.
[06:15] Sophie: awesome. I'll follow up in email with links and proposed kickoff times. thanks everyone.

End of call.

Notes/attachments referenced (not attached): POC_SOW_template.pdf, redwood-security-pack-2025.pdf, benchmark-harness-v1.zip, sample-configs/tgi-to-redwood.md

Ironcrest weekly pulse: bench debrief & routing decisions

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-01
Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood, AE); Liam O'Connor (Redwood, SE); Dr. Ana Valdez (Ironcrest, CTO); Samir Patel (Ironcrest, Lead ML Eng); Jordan Reyes (Ironcrest, Platform Eng)

Summary: Quick sync on week-two POC bench results vs incumbent (NimbusAI). We reviewed latency deltas, throughput headroom, cache behavior, and options for routing + dedicated slots. Agreed next steps for a focused head-to-head and to exchange raw CSVs and configs.

Topics: bench numbers, kv cache effects, quantization profile, routing fallback, dedicated slot request, SOC2/KMS Qs, scheduling of deep-dive.

Action items (recap) at end.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — we want to run through the numbers from last nights runs, talk about what changed since the midweek tune, and agree next steps. hi Ana, Samir, Jordan.
[00:23] Ana: Hey Maya, thanks. yes we're tight on time today, got a leadership sync after this but wanted to get the numbers and anything that blocks our gating decisions.
[00:37] Samir: hey all. We're primarily interested in the p95 delta vs Nimbus, and also the end-to-end throughput at peak traffic.
[00:50] Liam: perfect. quick note — the runs we did were with Redwood hosted config: batching=auto, batch_size cap 64, kv cache on, quantize=8-bit dynamic, and routing rules set to prefer low-latency nodes in us-west. baseline run from Ironcrest used Nimbus default with their autoscaler and no kv caching.
[01:13] Jordan: okay good to know, that difference might explain the throughput gap we saw. can you just run numbers?
[01:20] Maya: yes. headline: median token latency improved, p95 for short-chat workload was 82ms on Redwood vs 128ms on Nimbus under the same concurrency profile. throughput — we measured sustained 720 requests/sec on Redwood nodes at 1024-token max with 8 workers, Nimbus sustained about 470 rps before they started shedding.
[01:48] Ana: those are promising numbers. can you confirm tokenization/parsing was identical? we had a prior case where tokenization discrepancies made apples-to-oranges.
[02:01] Liam: good call. we ran the exact same prompt corpus and tokenizer binary; small variance came from their pre-processing microservice which adds a 5-8ms overhead, so we stripped that out for the head-to-head numbers reported.
[02:18] Samir: hmm, the p95 improvement looks great but the tail — did you capture p99? we care about the worst-case for user journeys.
[02:27] Maya: p99 was 310ms on Redwood vs 660ms on Nimbus for that short-chat set under the 700rps sustained test. we think the difference is KV cache hit patterns and our routing — Redwood's warm KV cache avoided repeated KV loads on many sessions.
[02:46] Jordan: what about larger context lengths? our internal tests use up to 2048 tokens for some flows.
[02:53] Liam: we ran a 2k token pass too — throughput dropped (expected) but the relative latency delta shrank: p95 about 320ms Redwood vs 410ms Nimbus at 250rps. So Redwood still ahead but margin reduces as context grows.
[03:15] Ana: were these runs on shared hosted capacity? we've been debating dedicated slots for stable tail SLOs.
[03:23] Maya: yes these were hosted. we can provision dedicated slots — that gives you pinned GPU capacity, predictable throughput, and you'll likely see the p99 tighten up. we can estimate the committed capacity needed based on your peak qps.
[03:36] Samir: any data on cost delta? throughput is great but we can't double our inference bill.
[03:42] Maya: initial cost estimate: with batching and kv caching enabled Redwood lowered token-unit cost by ~28% vs Nimbus for this workload. exact numbers in the CSV I'll share. Dedicated price has commit options to reduce unit cost further.
[03:56] Jordan: how much of the improvement is from quantization? we've observed accuracy regressions at 8-bit on our CCD model.
[04:03] Liam: good catch — quantization contributed about 8-12% of the token cost savings and 5-10% latency improvement for the decoder-heavy pieces. but we tested eval prompts and didn't see accuracy drift beyond your tolerance on the sampled set; however we'll run more evals with your production samples.
[04:22] Ana: please run the evals; accuracy is a hard requirement. also we need SOC2 evidence and KMS integration info for audit.
[04:30] Maya: we'll share the security pack — SOC2 Type II attestation, SSO/SAML docs, and KMS/HSM options.
[04:36] Samir: routing — you mentioned fallback policies. in a cross-region outage we need deterministic fallback to an equivalent model; can Redwood do model variant fallback automatically?
[04:46] Liam: yes — our smart routing can define policy: prefer region A, fallback to quantized variant in region B, fallback to lower-latency smaller model, etc. we can make it per-route and tie it to SLA thresholds.
[04:58] Jordan: curious — when fallback to smaller model happens, what's observability surface? we want to track per-request which variant served it.
[05:06] Liam: tracing header on requests, route-level metrics, and token-level cost breakdown in the console. you can set alerts on regressions in quality or latency.
[05:18] Maya: small aside — we also captured error rates. Redwood error rate during the sustained 720rps test was 0.14% vs Nimbus 0.9% (timed out and 5xx).
[05:30] Samir: that's a meaningful operational delta. ok so next up for us is to run the disabled-KV cache head-to-head because our flow can't rely on cache for privacy reasons.
[05:41] Liam: yep, that's on our side to execute. we'll run the 2-hour head-to-head with kv disabled and identical autoscale behavior.
[05:48] Ana: can you also test with single-model pinned (no model variant fallback) to emulate our compliance constraints?
[05:56] Maya: yes — we'll run one pass pinned to the same model family and same weights, then another pass with fallback enabled so you can compare.
[06:05] Jordan: on the dedicated slot ask — what's the lead time if we want to trial a dedicated GPU pool? we might want to spin a small reserved pool for two weeks.
[06:14] Maya: we can provision a short reserved pool (burstable) in about 48 hours for dev/demo. For enterprise private deployment (VPC) it's longer, typically 2-3 weeks for network setup and KMS integration.
[06:26] Samir: network question — if we go dedicated in hosted but within our VPC peering, can we use our own KMS keys?
[06:33] Liam: yes, we support customer-managed keys via supported KMS providers for dedicated and private deployments. audit logs support and HSM options available.
[06:41] Ana: good. any red flags you saw in the runs?
[06:45] Liam: nothing major, but one anomaly: around minute 37 of the long run we saw a spike in queuing time. digging in, small GC pause in the model worker and a routing rebalance during a node rotation. We have mitigations: pre-warm and stagger node rotations, and improved GC settings for the runtime.
[07:07] Maya: we can also pin a small buffer of spare workers during your peak window to avoid rotations then.
[07:13] Samir: about the dev test dataset we'll upload — should we anonymize or can Redwood handle PII?
[07:20] Maya: Redwood will handle PII per enterprise terms, but for bench sharing it's simpler if you anonymize payloads. we'll sign the NDA addendum for raw traffic if needed.
[07:31] Jordan: ok we'll prepare an anonymized slice first.
[07:35] Ana: on the security pack — send it to our security inbox and I'll route.
[07:40] Maya: will do.
[07:43] [08:00] Liam: quick note about the CSV — columns included: timestamp, endpoint, model_variant, tokens_in, tokens_out, p50, p95, p99, node_id, cache_hit, error_code. we'll attach it.
[08:13] Samir: perfect. can you also include the raw histograms for tail latency, not just percentiles?
[08:18] Liam: yes, histograms and raw samples.
[08:22] Maya: ok wrapping up, recap and owners: Maya share CSV & security pack; Liam run KV-disabled head-to-head; Samir/Jordan provide sample traffic and open VPC peering request; schedule deep-dive for routing.
[08:38] Ana: sounds good. one last question — competitor mentions: Nimbus claimed they could hit 800rps at 512 tokens in their latest private config; why did they plateau at 470rps in your run?
[08:51] Liam: likely because Nimbus runs heavier pre/post-processing and their default batch scheduler has a different latency-first policy which reduces throughput. Also their autoscaler cadence caused small hiccups under step-load. We did a small test enabling their throughput-optimized profile and they reached ~560rps but with increased tail latency.
[09:12] Samir: that's helpful. ok we'll review and sync again after the head-to-head. thanks everyone.

Recap & next steps (verbatim):
- Redwood to share raw CSV and runbook (Maya) by 2026-10-02.
- Redwood SE to run a 2-hour head-to-head with KV disabled (Liam) and report p50/p95/p99 + histograms by 2026-10-04.
- Ironcrest to provide anonymized production traffic sample and SSO test user (Samir/Jordan) by 2026-10-05.
- Schedule routing/fallback deep-dive 2026-10-06 17:00 UTC.

Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hearings; some technical terms might be transcribed imperfectly.

Prompt drift, lift & A/B compare — demo (Orchid Tech)

Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-11-09
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Orchid Head ML), Daniel Kim (Eng Manager), Alex Ruiz (Data Eng), Sam Ortega (Product)

Summary: Short demo of Redwood's Eval/Quality monitoring workflows (prompt sets, regression alerts, pairwise A/B compare) and discussion about running a short pilot. Customer cares about drift detection, low-latency inference, and SOC2 compliance.

Topics covered: console walkthrough, API snippet for sending eval telemetry, setting up regression alerts, running AB comparisons and reporting lift, security questions (SSO, KMS, audit logs), pilot scope and next steps.

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, welcome, thanks for taking time. I'm Maya from Redwood, and Liam's gonna walk through the Evalops and A/B compare features. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya: Good, thanks. Quick context: we're shipping a recommendations assistant and worried about prompt drift and unexpected negative regressions when we change models or quantize. We want automated alerts and a way to compare two model variants across our prompt set.
[00:18] Liam: Perfect. That's exactly what this demo is for. We'll show Console, the API flow for sending prompt telemetry and the Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization.
[00:27] Daniel: Quick Q — will this require hosting our prompts in your cloud? We have residency reqs.
[00:33] Maya: Good question. For the hosted pilot we can keep telemetry masked and we also support VPC/private deployment options if data residency is a hard req. For pilot we usually do a sandbox with RBAC and customer-managed KMS.
[00:44] Alex: Are audit logs available for each inference call? Our audit team asks for per-request logs, not aggregates.
[00:49] Liam: Yes, we log per-request metadata — not full PII by default — and export to your S3 or SIEM. There's an audit-log toggle in the console. Note sometimes the auto-transcription says "KV cash" — the runtime actually exposes KV cache metrics, sorry for that, 
[00:58] Maya: ha, yeah transcriptty stuff.
[01:05] [01:15] Liam: Alright I'm sharing screen, Console -> Evalops -> Prompt Sets. You can see a named prompt set for "checkout-recs" used in today's sandbox. We show baseline metrics: pass-rate, avg token cost, 95th latency.
[01:30] Priya: The pass-rate metric — is that per-example rubric, or do you support pairwise human labels?
[01:36] Liam: Both. You can upload a golden set (human labels) or use pairwise comparisons which is useful for A/B lift measurement. The pairwise UI will sample outputs from both variants and surface aggregated win rates and effect size.
[01:50] Sam: And that handles traffic splits? We want to run 10% of live traffic to a new quantized model.
[01:56] Liam: Yep — in Deployments you can configure traffic split, canary windows, and rollback policies. The Evalops alerting can be bound to those splits so you get early signals.
[02:08] [02:15] Daniel: Interrupt — how do you compute statistical significance on small sample sizes? We don't have huge traffic on some intents.
[02:22] Liam: We use a bootstrap-based pairwise comparison and show confidence intervals. For small samples we flag low-powered tests and suggest increasing sampling or running targeted prompts.
[02:35] Priya: Is there an integration with our existing eval framework? We use an internal notebook and W&B for tracking.
[02:41] Maya: We have an API and a small Python client to push eval telemetry. We can also export CSVs/JSON that you can import into W&B.
[02:51] [03:00] Liam: Showing the API: POST /v1/eval/observations — you send prompt_id, model_variant, tokens_in/out, response_text, score fields. We also accept custom labels and metadata so you can attach session ids, user cohort, etc.
[03:14] Alex: Does sending telemetry increase quota/billing?
[03:18] Maya: Telemetry is generally counted as metered events but we can bundle it into pilot credits. Cost for telemetry is negligible compared to generation cost.
[03:28] [03:45] Liam: Back to Console — here's the regression alerts page. You set an alert: scope (prompt-set or route), metric (win-rate, latency, pass-rate), threshold, lookback window, and action (email, webhook, auto-rollback).
[03:58] Priya: Can the threshold be based on relative change? e.g., >5% drop in pass-rate vs baseline?
[04:04] Liam: Yes, you can use relative delta or absolute thresholds. There's built-in anomaly detection too which looks for unusual distribution shifts.
[04:13] Daniel: What do alerts include? We need the sample failing prompts for triage.
[04:18] Liam: Alerts include top failing prompts, diffed responses, token-level cost delta, and a link to pairwise A/B view. You can export failing cases as CSV.
[04:26] [04:40] Sam: Do you support automatic correction like rerouting to stable model if the new one fails?
[04:45] Maya: Yes, fallback policies — route traffic to a pinned stable variant or to a lower-cost fall-back. You can chain policies: fallback to dedicated capacity in another region if latency breaches SLA.
[04:58] Priya: Security questions: SSO? SAML? KMS?
[05:04] Maya: SSO via SAML/Okta, SCIM provisioning, RBAC at project and token level, customer-managed KMS/HSM for encryption at rest. SOC2 Type II documentation and ISO certs are available in the security pack we'll share.
[05:18] Daniel: Great. On the technical side, we care about perf for short prompts — 8-16 token completions, 95th latency under 120ms if possible. Can you get us latencies for a quantized Llama-style model?
[05:29] Liam: We can. Quantized variants often save cost but can add tail-latency depending on kernel selection. Our runtime uses sequence-aware kernels and async batching — for short prompts we can keep latency low. We'll run a focused benchmark for your prompt distribution.
[05:44] [06:00] Liam: Now demoing pairwise A/B compare. I create an experiment: base-v1 vs quantized-v1, attach the "checkout-recs" prompt set, set 7-day window, and choose pairwise as metric. You can choose stratify by user cohort (new vs returning).
[06:17] Priya: In pairwise, how do you label winner/loser? Is it based on rubric or human judge?
[06:22] Liam: You can use automated rubric functions (soft-match, semantic similarity) or push to a human labeling queue. The UI shows both automated and hand-labeled breakdowns.
[06:33] Alex: Does the system cache previous outputs so pairwise compares stable results? We want deterministic comparisons.
[06:38] Liam: We support prefix and KV cache controls — you can pin KV cache behavior or clear caches for test runs to make them comparable. Also we store outputs per observation which helps exact diffing.
[06:50] [07:05] Priya: We have some red flags — we sometimes see hallucinations that are cost-insensitive, we'd like an alert on an increase in hallucination rate. Can Redwood measure hallucinations automatically?
[07:15] Liam: Hallucination detection is tricky but you can plug in custom automatic validators — e.g., fact-checker model or NER matchers — and compute a hallucination metric. We also support rule-based checks for forbidden content.
[07:30] [07:45] Daniel: Ok let's walk through an example. Priya uploads a 10-sample golden set now (pretend).
[07:50] Priya: Uploading — send via S3 link in the chat.
[07:55] Alex: (mumble) link posted.
[08:02] Liam: I see it. Importing the golden set — mapping columns now. The system detected expected_field names but some columns are fuzzy. There may be a bit of parsing errors in CSVs so we often ask for a tiny sample first.
[08:20] Priya: noted.
[08:25] [08:45] Liam: I'm creating a regression alert: scope=checkout-recs, metric=pass-rate, threshold=relative_drop>5% vs baseline, action=webhook+email. Saving. The UI now shows an expected time-to-detect chart based on current traffic.
[08:59] Sam: Nice. Will the webhook contain the raw failing responses or just IDs?
[09:04] Liam: The webhook payload includes top failing cases and a link to download the CSV. You can opt in to include full responses (we mask PII unless requested).
[09:15] [09:30] Maya: Quick aside — we sometimes see customers mention Pinecone for vector store. We do embeddings integration but for evalops the important part is stable prompt ids and consistent scoring.
[09:43] Priya: Any pitfalls we should know when running quantized models in production?
[09:48] Liam: Two common issues: 1) small distribution shift in tokenization/decoding can change pass-rate, 2) some quantization backends increase p95 latency. Optimize suggests quantization profiles per workload and will warn if latency increases are expected.
[10:05] [10:20] Daniel: Can we connect Redwood's eval alerts to PagerDuty?
[10:24] Maya: Yes webhook -> PagerDuty, Slack, Opsgenie supported out of the box.
[10:30] Alex: For the A/B results, how do you surface effect size? I want to give execs a short one-liner like "+3.2% lift on purchase intent with p<0.05"
[10:38] Liam: The summary card computes win-rate and Cohen's d and reports p-values from bootstrap. The export includes the test-statistic and CI so you can craft that one-liner.
[10:50] [11:05] Priya: If we do a pilot, we expect a simple scope: 2-week bench with our prompt set, a pairing comparing base vs quantized, and an ops runbook for rollout. Cost?
[11:17] Maya: For pilot we propose a credit-backed sandbox: Redwood covers initial telemetry and evaluation costs; you cover generation and optional dedicated capacity if you want a reserved pool. We'll send pricing in the SOW.
[11:30] [11:45] Liam: Quick show of the AB compare report — it's got waterfall view showing which prompts contributed most to lift (or loss). You can filter by cohorts and narrow down to specific intents.
[11:58] Priya: That waterfall is super helpful — helps prioritize prompts to rewrite or add guardrails.
[12:06] Daniel: Are there SDKs? We prefer a Python SDK for pushing observations server-side.
[12:11] Maya: Yes Python and Node SDKs, plus curl for quick tests. We'll share the sample scripts in the follow-up.
[12:22] [12:40] Liam: One small demo glitch — the live sampling UI had a small lag, the transcript might show duplicate rows. UI is still beta but functionality is stable.
[12:52] Sam: Noted.
[13:00] [13:15] Priya: Another constraint — we have internal legal asks re: data retention. We need 30-day retention of raw responses, and then redact. Can you set retention per project?
[13:26] Maya: Yes retention is configurable per workspace; auto-redaction hooks are available and we can provide export before deletion.
[13:36] Alex: Also want to make sure KMS keys rotate per policy and that audit logs show key usage.
[13:42] Liam: KMS integrations emit key usage logs and we can surface that in audit exports.
[13:52] [14:10] Maya: Ok wrapping up demo portion. Quick recap: Console shows prompt sets and pairwise AB compare, regression alerts with failing-cases export, traffic-split-aware monitoring, and integrations for SSO/KMS/audit. Pilot plan is 2-week bench + AB compare + runbook. Next steps listed in chat.
[14:35] Daniel: One more — how long to get sandbox access and credentials?
[14:39] Maya: We can provision a sandbox within 2 business days after we get a PO/credentials and the sample data. For the benchmark run Liam will need the sample prompt-set and a small telemetry dump.
[14:52] Priya: We'll aim to upload by Wednesday.
[15:00] [15:10] Liam: I'll run the bench and share a spreadsheet with latency, token-cost, and win-rate columns. Expect one consolidated report within 48 hours of the run.
[15:22] Maya: Great. Thanks all. We'll follow up with SOW and the security pack.
[15:28] Priya: Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

HelioCore Analytics - VPC Onramp Readiness Discovery

Intro/discovery for private deployment options. Customer runs regulated healthcare analytics, needs region-constrained VPC onramp, SOC2 controls, and a narrow egress policy. Discussed peering vs PrivateLink/Private Endpoint, transit gateway patterns, DNS and route tables, and dedicated capacity tradeoffs. Agreed to collect network diagrams and schedule a pilot-run SRE workshop.
VPC peering vs PrivateLink/Private Endpoint
Transit gateway and inter-region peering
Egress/egress control and NATing
Regional model availability & data residency
SLA and dedicated capacity considerations
Security: KMS, audit logs, SOC2
Priya Shah: draft VPC onramp checklist + sample route table by 2027-01-18
Marta Ruiz: share current network diagram and CIDR blocks by 2027-01-14
Evan Morales: send pricing worksheet and Dedicated capacity SLAs by 2027-01-15
Redwood to review HelioCore network diagram and validate PrivateLink feasibility
Schedule SRE workshop (deep dive) week of 2027-01-25
Pilot request: 2-week Dedicated trial in eu-west-1 or us-east-1 to test latency/regional restrictions
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-11 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Evan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marta (HelioCore Head of Infra), Samir (Cloud Arch), Tori (Security), Devon (ML Platform)

[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro, I'm Evan on the account team at Redwood and Priya our SE will run through the networking bits.
[00:18] Priya: hi all, thanks. I know HelioCore does a lot with PHI-adjacent datasets so we wanna understand your onramp needs before we talk hosting options. Marta, can you give quick context on current infra?
[00:29] Marta: sure. We're mainly in aws, primary regions us-east-1 and eu-west-1. We have a transit gateway between our core VPCs and a handful of segmented env VPCs. The models will run against de-identified records but compliance wants no egress to public endpoints, and region residency for logs.
[00:45] Samir: also to add, we prefer to avoid internet-facing endpoints for model inference; want private endpoints or peering into vendor networks. Timeline is Q2 pilot, production Q3 if validation goes well.
[01:02] Priya: got it. So two axes: network connectivity (peering, PrivateLink/private endpoint, transit), and region/residency constraints. We support Hosted, Dedicated, and Private — for your constraints, Private (VPC onramp) or Dedicated in a customer VPC look likely.
[01:20] Tori: Clarify: when you say Dedicated, is that in Redwood's cloud or our VPC? We need single-tenant and KMS integration.
[01:28] Evan: good question. Dedicated can be Redwood-managed but isolated, or we can do Private with control plane separated and deployment into your VPC via PrivateLink and private endpoints. KMS/HSM integrations are supported in Private — we do Bring Your Own Key patterns.
[01:43] Devon: spelling note, previously we saw references to KV cache in your docs — is that cached on your side or in our VPC? We need to make sure nothing PHI-esque is persisted externally.
[01:54] Priya: the KV cache term sometimes transcribed badly — it's KV cache, key-value cache, and for Private deployments it's contained in the customer's subnet. For Hosted it's on Redwood infra but we can enable ephemeral-only modes.
[02:12] Marta: ok that's helpful. Can we go into peering vs PrivateLink tradeoffs? We run a transit gateway already.
[02:20] Priya: yeah. Peering (VPC peering) is simple but doesn't scale well across many accounts/regions — route propagation via transit gateway is cleaner if you already have it. PrivateLink / Private Endpoint gives you endpoint IPs in your subnet and avoids cross-account route table complexity, but needs NLBs and more setup on the service side. Both can satisfy no-public-egress if configured with strict route tables.
[02:45] Samir: How about inter-region traffic? If we pin to eu-west-1 for data residency, but need failover, can Redwood replicate models across regions or fallback to a different region without crossing data boundaries?
[02:58] Priya: we have region-aware policies. For Private deployments we provision nodes in the region you require; if you need active/active across regions we can do that but it requires agreement on data replication flows. For strict residency we can limit failover to read-only queued requests and route users to region-local compute. There's also model variants pinned to regions.
[03:21] Tori: Audit logs — do the request/response logs stay in our account?
[03:26] Evan: in Private, yes, the control/data plane logs can be delivered into your logging stack. We support CloudWatch/S3 audits and can integrate with your SIEM. For Dedicated we can also stream logs to your destinations depending on contract.
[03:40] Marta: egress policy — we want zero public egress from the inference subnets. How does tokenization or telemetry call out?
[03:49] Priya: telemetry is optional. By default telemetry is disabled for Private. For Hosted we do some aggregated metrics; for Dedicated we can toggle telemetry and deliver metrics to your VPC. Tokenization (like embedding generation) can be done fully inside the VPC.
[04:04] Samir: routing detail: if we use TGW peering, do you require overlapping CIDRs? we have tight CIDR allocations.
[04:11] Priya: we cannot overlap — CIDR disjointness is required for peering. For overlaps we typically recommend PrivateLink / Private Endpoint since it uses endpoint IPs in your subnet and doesn't require route overlap.
[04:25] Devon: performance — latency SLOs and throughput. We're serving sub-200ms tails on some endpoints. Can Dedicated meet that?
[04:33] Priya: Dedicated gives predictable throughput and lower tail latency due to reserved capacity. In many customer workloads we've seen median latencies well under 100ms for small models in colocated regions; large models obviously have higher token latencies. We'll propose a sizing and run a two-week pilot to validate tails.
[04:51] Marta: budget — Dedicated sounds costlier. What's the economics vs Hosted?
[04:55] Evan: Hosted is pay-as-you-go, lower onboarding; Dedicated is reserved capacity (monthly commit). Private adds infra and networking work but gives you control for compliance. We'll send a cost comparison sheet with estimated unit economics for your expected qps.
[05:08] Tori: SSO and RBAC — can we use SAML and map roles?
[05:12] Priya: yes. SAML SSO is supported for Console access; RBAC can be mapped to your identity provider. For Private deployments the control plane can be configured to federate to your IdP.
[05:24] Samir: DNS — if we create PrivateLink endpoints, we usually rewrite DNS to point to endpoint addresses. Does Redwood provide guidance for split-horizon?
[05:33] Priya: we can provide a DNS guide. For PrivateLink we provide an endpoint DNS name you can resolve internally. For peering patterns you must manage route tables and possibly internal ALB/NLB entries. We'll include recommended route table entries in the checklist.
[05:50] Evan: quick sanity check — stakeholders for the pilot?
[05:54] Marta: devon will own the ML runbooks, Samir the network tasks, and Tori will sign off on compliance. I'll coordinate scheduling.
[06:03] Evan: great. Priya, could you walk through a tentative network pattern for Transit Gateway + PrivateLink?
[06:09] Priya: sure. Sketching: you keep your TGW as the hub, create a dedicated subnet for Redwood endpoints in each region — either via peering into a Redwood-managed account or via PrivateLink. If using PrivateLink, we provision a service behind NLBs in Redwood infra and publish endpoint services; you then create VPC endpoints in your subnets. Route tables point internal app traffic to the endpoint. For TGW you'd associate the app VPC attachments and propagate routes. We also recommend security groups that restrict source CIDRs to your app subnet.
[06:42] Samir: one more — egress to other AWS services (S3) for model artifacts. We need to ensure artifact access doesn't leave region.
[06:50] Priya: we can either keep artifacts in your S3 and mount via VPC endpoints (S3 gateway or VPC endpoint) or push artifacts to region-local storage. We'll include artifact workflows in the checklist.
[07:03] Tori: encryption at rest? KMS with CMKs?
[07:06] Priya: yes, BYOK via KMS is supported for Private. You can bring CMKs and we can encrypt model caches and logs with that key. For Hosted we manage keys unless you use tokenization or special agreements.
[07:18] Marta: are there any major gotchas with PrivateLink in multi-account setups?
[07:23] Priya: mostly around endpoint quotas and cross-account sharing. You'll need endpoint service acceptance for cross-account, and there are per-region endpoint quotas; we can help with quota increases. Also NLB health checks need to be allowed from your subnets.
[07:38] Devon: small tangent — model quantization/latency. If we need 8-bit quantized models, does Redwood handle that or do we need to provide?
[07:46] Priya: Redwood supports quantized model variants and we'll recommend model flavors as part of Optimize. For Private deployments we can load quantized variants to meet latency/cost targets.
[07:58] Evan: OK, I wanna recap and confirm deliverables. Marta, you said you'll share the network diagram and CIDRs. Priya will produce a VPC-onramp checklist. I'll send pricing and SLA docs. We'll aim to schedule the SRE workshop week of Jan 25. Anything to add?
[08:14] Marta: can you also include a short runbook for certificate rotation and NLB health checks?
[08:20] Priya: yes, we'll include cert rotation notes and NLB health check guidance.
[08:24] Tori: also include SOC2 artifacts and a copy of the SOC report if possible behind an NDA.
[08:30] Evan: we'll share SOC2 + ISO docs via the secure doc portal; we'll need an NDA before the full report.
[08:37] Samir: one last networking question — if our CIDRs are overlapping with Redwood test accounts, can we get dedicated peering accounts?
[08:44] Priya: yes, we can provision a customer-dedicated account to avoid overlaps; that's part of Private onramp setups.
[08:51] Devon: pilot sizing — can you propose instance types? Our workloads are medium token sizes, concurrency ~20.
[08:58] Priya: we'll size based on qps and model. We'll propose a few SKU options in the pricing worksheet and highlight target latency/throughput.
[09:09] Evan: great. we'll wrap up with next steps and owners.

[09:15] (meeting transitions to logistics: agreements, NDA, scheduling and brief back-and-forth confirming times)

[45:12] Evan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the checklist and schedule.
[45:20] Marta: thanks, bye.

Notes: transcript contains typical ASR errors: "K V cash" instead of KV cache, product names sometimes lowercased, occasional speaker attribution drift.

Request RootCause Hypothesis Lab - Veridian Labs

Redwood AE/SE ran a lab-style walkthrough of the Console's request forensics, tracing, and error analysis features. Conversation focused on how to map request paths, identify root causes (model fallback, KV cache misses, routing), secure data in transit for VPC/private deployments, and scope a 2-week POC to reproduce a high-severity production error. Customer asked detailed SSO/KMS/KV cache questions and requested runbook examples and a small benchmark/trace set to validate behavior.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Gupta (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Rios (Veridian), Jonas Lee (Veridian CTO), Priya Menon (SRE), Sam Ortiz (Product), Lina Zhao (Data Privacy)

[00:00] Ethan Morales: hey everyone, thanks for making time, i'm ethan from redwood inference, and with me is priya our solutions engineer. we wanted to run a hands-on lab, um, to go through request-level forensics in the console — the trace maps, request logs, and how we typically debug root cause across fallbacks and kv cache behavior.
[00:18] Jonas Lee: thanks, ethan. high level, we had a sev last week where outputs went stale then we saw a spike in token cost. so main things: why did fallback trigger, where did latency come from, and how to avoid in future.
[00:35] Priya Gupta: yep, that's perfect. we'll start with a quick demo of a request timeline — the hop map — then we'll pull a couple of example traces that show a model fallback, a kv cache miss, and an infra retry. i'll also show how to link to the raw request logs and the model-side metrics.
[00:50] Dr. Maya Rios: quick one, is this the hosted console or our private deployment? our security team will want to understand what telemetry leaves the VPC.
[00:58] Ethan Morales: good call. for the demo we'll use a sandbox tenant on hosted, but all the artifacts and the features are the same for Dedicated and Private; we'll call out what changes for VPC / private control plane.
[01:12] Priya Gupta: starting screen share now — ok, here's the request list, you can see filters on model, route, status. i'm going to pick a failed request from last week — see this one flagged with high token spend and an error code 504-ish.
[01:30] [01:30] Priya Gupta: the trace timeline — we show time per stage: routing -> model call -> kv cache lookup -> response assembly. you can expand the model call to see kernel-level timings, queue time, and the selected execution variant, e.g., quantized vs fp16.
[01:47] Sam Ortiz: when you say 'kv cache' is that the prefix cache? or is it the per-request kv? we have a large prompt prefix, and sometimes we'd prefer cache hits.
[01:58] Priya Gupta: it's both — prefix cache is our automatic prefix/KV caching: if we detect repeating prefixes we cache KV pages. there's also explicit per-request KV cache control via the SDK headers. we surface the hit/miss at the trace level.
[02:14] Priya Menon: can you show an example of a miss leading to longer model time? that's what we saw — long tail on a subset of requests.
[02:21] Priya Gupta: sure, zooming in — here's a trace with a miss: you can see the kv lookup returned cold, which pushed more context to the model and the kernel selection jumped to a longer-path execution; see the extra 200–350 ms there, and token spend went up because more decoding happened.
[02:40] [02:40] Dr. Maya Rios: i notice the model fallback in the trace, it tried a smaller variant first?
[02:47] Priya Gupta: in this tenant the routing policy is cost-prefer then latency-fallback. so it tried a cheaper quantized variant, but because of the longer context it timed out and the router retried to a larger fp16 model. that retry doubled the per-request cost.
[03:05] Jonas Lee: is there a way to set a hard SLO that avoids retries? we sometimes prefer a fast, slightly lower quality answer over paying double.
[03:13] Priya Gupta: yes — in routing policies you can set max retry budget and fallback behavior: either prefer cheaper models with best-effort, or fail fast to a configured error code. also you can pin a model variant per route to avoid any fallback.
[03:31] Ethan Morales: quick commercial note — Dedicated capacity gives you more predictable throughput so you see fewer kernel hops and retries under load; for cost-sensitive flows many customers run a small dedicated pool for critical routes.
[03:45] Lina Zhao: on data privacy — if we do Dedicated or Private, does telemetry like request text and traces remain in our VPC?
[03:52] Ethan Morales: with Private deployments the control plane is customer-managed and telemetry can be routed to your internal logging — you can choose to redact request text at ingest or only store metadata. for Hosted we (Redwood) retain traces per the retention policy but we offer field-level redaction and bring-your-own-kms for encrypting at rest.
[04:15] [04:15] Priya Gupta: back to the trace — here's a combined view with the console's error correlation: we show error clusters (timeouts, model OOM, kv miss) and you can click to see all requests in that cluster and to export a CSV for downstream triage.
[04:31] Sam Ortiz: how accurate is the clustering? we've seen noise in automated clusters before.
[04:36] Priya Gupta: clustering is heuristic-based and you can supply custom rules — e.g., cluster by substring in stack, by error code range, or by top-of-stack fingerprint. we also support manual labeling and you can feed labels back into the quality monitor.
[04:51] [05:00] Ethan Morales: let's walk through a root-cause hypothesis: the sev looked like token burn + stale outputs. hypothesis one: prefix cache miss combined with quantized variant timeout caused retry; hypothesis two: upstream client sent duplicate requests causing double billing; hypothesis three: model regression in that version increased decode steps. we'll show how to validate each with traces and logs.
[05:24] [05:24] Priya Gupta: validating the cache miss: filter traces by kv_hit=false and by route. here's the histogram of request latencies for kv_hit vs kv_miss — you can see the 95th jumps.
[05:36] Dr. Maya Rios: can we integrate these traces with our existing SRE pager system? we want alerts when key patterns appear.
[05:42] Priya Gupta: yes, you can export alerts via webhook or forward anomalies into your monitoring (PagerDuty, Datadog). console has an alert rule builder: example rule - > if cluster 'kv_miss' > 3% for 5m -> fire webhook.
[06:00] [06:00] Jonas Lee: network question: with Private, do we require VPC peering or is it egress? we have strict egress rules.
[06:08] Ethan Morales: for Private you run a control plane in your VPC; data plane stays in your environment. we support IP allowlist, VPC peering, and egress narrows; we'll share the network diagram. for hosted, we support VPC peering and customer-provided NAT for egress control.
[06:30] Priya Menon: what about key management? we need to use our HSM, not Redwood KMS.
[06:36] Priya Gupta: BYOK (bring your own key) is supported for Private and Dedicated via integrations with major KMS/HSM offerings; we can show the config snippet.
[06:46] [07:00] Priya Gupta: next demo - request playback: you can replay a historical request into a sandbox model and see how different model variants respond, plus measure token delta and latency. i'm going to replay the failing request into two variants.
[07:15] [07:15] Priya Gupta: replay 1 -> quantized v1: it times out at ~1.2s; replay 2 -> fp16 v2: completes in 0.6s but costs 2x tokens. console shows per-token breakdown.
[07:30] Sam Ortiz: can we automate replay against a set of golden requests nightly?
[07:35] Priya Gupta: yes — we have a replay API and scheduled jobs; many customers run nightly replays against canary model variants to detect regressions.
[07:46] [08:00] Dr. Maya Rios: about retention — how long do traces live? our privacy policy is strict.
[08:06] Ethan Morales: retention is configurable per-tenant; default 30 days for hosted, but you can increase or decrease and set redaction rules. for Private you control retention entirely.
[08:20] Priya Gupta: moving on, here's the request inspector which shows the raw request payload, request headers (we obfuscate tokens), and the model prompt slice. note sometimes the transcription will show 'speaker 6' because of upload metadata, that's normal.
[08:40] [08:40] Jonas Lee: we also saw an unusual pattern where a batch of requests had identical client request-ids but different IPs — could that be a client-side retry?
[08:50] Priya Gupta: identical request-id with different client IP usually means client retried without dedup; our logs show dedup keys and time windows. you can set idempotency windows per-route to avoid double billing.
[09:05] [09:05] Priya Gupta: switching to the error waterfall view — this shows the order errors occurred in the trace chain; you can annotate and then jump to the request in raw logs. you can also attach a runbook link to a cluster so responders see the recommended triage steps.
[09:22] Sam Ortiz: would love a starter runbook we can adapt.
[09:25] Priya Gupta: absolutely — i'll attach our 'request-failure-runbook' template to the follow-up.
[09:33] [09:33] Ethan Morales: quick question for the privacy/regs team — Lina, do you have constraints about storing PII inside traces?
[09:40] Lina Zhao: we avoid storing raw user text unless necessary; if we must, it needs to be encrypted with our key and retained under 90 days and be auditable. also need SOC2 evidence.
[09:51] Ethan Morales: that's fine — we'll mark those fields as redacted by default and we'll include the SOC2 docs in the package.
[10:00] [10:00] Priya Gupta: jumping to live demo of lazy prefix caching: here's a time series showing savings after enabling lazy caching on a route — token cost per request drops as hits increase. you can configure cache TTL and eviction.
[10:22] Dr. Maya Rios: is eviction LRU?

[14:21] [14:30] Priya Gupta: bringing up the test harness: here are the sample traces we recommend sending — 50 failing requests, 100 normal, and a burst scenario. we'll run them through the replay and compare quantized vs fp16 and show cost deltas.
[14:45] Sam Ortiz: for the POC success criteria, propose: reproduce the failure, show 10–20% cost improvement with caching/pinning, and demonstrate alerting tied to our PagerDuty.
[14:58] Ethan Morales: good, that'll be in the POC doc.
[15:05] [15:00] Priya Gupta: one more advanced view — the console exposes a model internals pane: token-level attention heatmaps and kernel switching events. helpful to understand when kernel choices inflate latency.

tenant hotkey localization and eviction fault-domain review with Hypha Systems

Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Recording: auto
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Ethan Chu (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Solutions), Ravi Patel (Hypha CTO), Leah Moreno (Hypha Platform), Omar Diaz (Hypha SRE)

Summary:
Quick architecture review focused on hotkey/localization behavior in the KV prefix cache for multi-tenant workloads, eviction strategies, fault-domain isolation, and tradeoffs between latency vs cost for on-prem/VPC deployments. Hypha has strict tenancy isolation and intermittent bursty traffic from search/autocomplete microservice. They want deterministic tail latency and safe shared caches.

Topics discussed:
- KV/prefix cache keys and entropy
- Hotkey localization and sharding (fault domains)
- Eviction policy and grace periods for tenants
- Prefetch heuristics and adaptive batching
- Quantization interaction with cacheable prefixes
- VPC/on-prem networking and KMS for cached payloads
- Rollback/fallback strategies (model variant vs cold start)

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: okay everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to make this a hands-on review of the hotkey behavior you saw in staging, right Ravi?
[00:10] Ravi: yeah thanks, we've been seeing a small number of tenants generate a ton of prefix hits, like 40% of requests hitting the same keyspace and that is spiking GPU utilization and causing tail latency for others.
[00:22] Ethan: got it. so just to set context, our prefix KV is sharded across pool nodes using a consistent hash ring per region. by default keys are hashed with murmur3 and we group by tenant id + prefix signature.
[00:35] Leah: slight interruption — in our setup tenants sometimes share session IDs across products which is making signature collisions more likely, so maybe the keying is too coarse.
[00:47] Priya: that's a good callout. when keys are coarse we get big hot buckets. one leaky thing we see in generated transcripts is that hashing with only tenant id loses the prompt-level entropy. we usually suggest tenantid:namespace:prefixhash.
[01:05] Omar: quick question, is the cache stored encrypted at rest when using Redwood Private on-prem? we need to know for audits.
[01:12] Sofia: yes, on Private we encrypt with customer KMS/HSM; however there was a note that metadata like tenant id may be stored separately for routing, that stuff can be redacted if you want.
[01:24] Ravi: great. so the problem concretely: Tenant A and B are fine but Tenant C has a hot feature — autocomplete with very small prompts, super low entropy — it dominates. we need fault-domain isolation so that one tenant's hotkeys don't evict others.
[01:38] Ethan: a few strategies we've used: separate hot-key partitions per-tenant (logical isolation), proactive replication of hot keys to dedicated hot-cache nodes, and TTL/eviction quotas per-tenant. each has tradeoffs: isolation reduces cold-start efficiency and increases memory overhead.
[01:54] Leah: replication sounds promising, can you walk through replication cost, and how it affects latency for first token?
[02:02] Ethan: replication adds memory copy & bandwidth; read latency can be lower because you avoid cross-node lookup, but writes to the cache need to be propagated — we do async replication for prefix loads so the write path is quick. there is a window where a hotspot is written to a node and other nodes will learn it in ~100-300ms depending on gossip.
[02:23] Ravi: that propagation window is ok if our tail SLO is 200ms p99; 300ms is a bit high. is there a way to make the learn faster?
[02:31] Priya: yes, we can do targeted prefetching when we detect a key jump in traffic. e.g., if a prefix crosses a threshold (requests/sec) we promote it to the hot lane and push to dedicated nodes synchronously. that's more CPU/bandwidth but keeps p99 low.
[02:46] Omar: do you have metrics on the push vs gossip tradeoff? like how many extra ops per second?
[02:52] Ethan: from our internal bench: targeted sync push increased network ops by ~12% for workloads with 5% hotspots, but decreased p99 by ~60ms on the overloaded cluster. numbers vary with seq length; very short prompts are dominated by KV lookup overhead.
[03:10] Leah: about key composition — we use LLM embeddings to normalize similar prompts into the same canonical key. will that break when you shard by hash?
[03:19] Priya: you can canonicalize first then hash. HM, one risk: semantic canonicalization can increase collisions unintentionally — if different tenants canonicalize to same value there is cross-tenant leakage. so canonicalization should include tenant namespace unless you purposely want cross-tenant cache sharing.
[03:36] Ravi: we definitely want tenant siloing. Hypha's audit requires per-tenant cache control.
[03:41] Sofia: then we recommend tenant:canonicalHash as the key. and also namespace isolation with enforcement at routing layer so your tenant's hot keys are pinned to that tenant's fault domain.
[03:53] Ethan: another lever is hybrid eviction: global LRU with per-tenant min-reserve + dynamic soft-limits. basically keep N entries guaranteed per tenant and allow burst overage up to M% that decays. prevents thrashing.
[04:07] Omar: sounds good in theory, but if a tenant has 100x more active keys do you have a risk of memory blowout?
[04:14] Ethan: yes, so we add tenant quotas and admission control; when a tenant exceeds budget we can either throttle prefetches, refuse to cache new prefixes, or route them to a lower-cost quantized model variant that has its own small cache.
[04:28] Ravi: you've mentioned quantized model fallback a few times — how does quantization affect cacheability of prefixes?
[04:35] Priya: short answer: cache entries are model-dependent because tokenization and KV states differ across model variants. if you fall back to a quantized 4-bit variant you need a separate cache namespace or you risk wrong KV shapes. that said, for short prefix hits where output is dominated by cached logits you can sometimes serve from a shared prefix cache but it's safer to segregate caches by model family and quant profile.
[04:58] Leah: operationally that means more memory, right?
[05:01] Ethan: yes more memory or tighter admission control. tradeoffs.
[05:06] Sofia: quick sanity check — Hypha is considering Private (on-prem) and also Dedicated in our hosted for DR. how are network latencies and cross-region prefetching handled in Private?
[05:16] Ethan: on Private you typically keep the KV cache local to the cluster. we support optional cross-cluster replication but it traverses VPC peering and will add 20-80ms depending on topology. for DR we recommend async cross-region replication with eventual consistency.
[05:32] Omar: KMS question again — if we replicate prefixes, are cached payloads encrypted with the same key and is that permitted across regions? compliance needs the same KMS policy.
[05:42] Priya: yes you can configure per-cluster KMS or a central KMS and we can support key wrapping for cross-region replication. that's common for customers with strict egress policies.
[05:52] Ravi: okay good. back to eviction — can you show a simple eviction policy we'd run for Hypha's workload?
[05:58] Ethan: sure here's a sketch we discussed: 1) per-tenant reserve = 1000 entries
2) global soft-limit per node = 80% of alloc
3) hot promotion threshold = 250 req/min for prefix
4) promotion copies to hot-lane with ttl 30m
5) decay multiplier 0.5 every 15m if not seen
6) admission rejection backpressure when tenant over budget -> route to quantized model variant

[06:26] Leah: that seems reasonable. what about instrumentation — what dashboards will show tenant eviction and eviction-caused misses?
[06:33] Priya: Redwood Console exposes per-tenant cache hit/miss, per-prefix hotlist, eviction reasons (LRU, quota, manual), and end-to-end latency broken down by KV lookup, model forward, and network. we can hook to your prom stack or push metrics to onboarding s3.
[06:49] Omar: do you expose the actual prefix keys in metrics? we need them masked for PII.
[06:55] Sofia: by default we hash prefix keys in telemetry and optionally redact tenant ids. you can set retention and redaction in the Console.
[07:03] Ravi: perfect. switching to batching — Hypha uses short seq lengths but high concurrency; what's Redwood's recommended batch sizing?
[07:11] Ethan: for short sequences batching helps throughput but increases latency due to waiting for batch fill. we recommend adaptive micro-batching: target batch latency budget of 8-12ms (waiting) for p50 improvements, and cap wait at 20ms to protect p99. dynamic batching policies per route are ideal.
[07:31] Leah: any interaction between batching and prefix caching? like if a batch contains mixed tenants?
[07:36] Priya: yes mixed-tenant batches complicate KV cache locality. we prefer tenant-aware batching: prefer to pack requests from same tenant or same shard into a batch. if not possible, ensure KV lookup happens before batch assembly so each request carries its KV context.
[07:55] Omar: what about eviction when batching creates bursts? we sometimes have synchronized bursts every hour.
[08:01] Ethan: for synchronized bursts we recommend smoothing via token-bucket rate shaping at ingress or temporary increase of hot-lane capacity. Also TTL hysteresis helps — avoid immediate eviction during bursts.
[08:12] Ravi: curious about measurement — how do you measure hit-rate accurately? it's tricky when ephemeral keys and canonicalization are in play.
[08:20] Priya: measure both logical hit-rate (post-canonicalization) and raw-key hit-rate. we also suggest synthetic benchmarks: replay traces and mount simulated tenants to compute stable hit-rate percentiles across time windows.
[08:33] Ethan: we can run a 24h synthetic run with Hypha's trace and show p50/p95/p99 for hit-rate and latency. that's part of the next steps.
[08:41] Leah: let's talk about safety: if we mistakenly canonicalize across tenants we could leakage. show me config knobs to enforce tenant-segregated canonicalization.
[08:49] Priya: it's a simple config flag: canonicalizeWithinTenant = true. defaults to false for customers who want cross-tenant warming. set to true for Hypha. we also have audit logs for canonicalization decisions.
[09:00] Omar: good. any discussion on cache key size / key hashing collisions? we had one incident where murmur3 collisions showed up in a dev cluster.
[09:08] Ethan: collisions are possible in 32-bit hashes at high scale. we recommend 64-bit hashes or salted hashes with tenant-specific salt; salted hashing reduces chance of collision and prevents collision-based information leaks between tenants.
[09:21] Ravi: can you do deterministic rerouting on hash collision detection? like if two keys have same hash, detect and push to an overflow bucket?
[09:28] Ethan: yes we support overflow buckets and we also store the full key with the hashed index to detect false positives. that adds memory but keeps correctness.
[09:37] Priya: also we can move to content-addressable storage where key is full digest and index is a prefix, but that's heavier.
[09:44] Leah: switching to networking: for on-prem we will likely want local cache-only with occasional writes to central analytics. what's the recommended architecture for private clusters?
[09:53] Ethan: recommended: 1) local KV + hot-lane nodes in each cluster 2) local KMS for encryption at rest 3) async cross-cluster replication of hot keys to DR cluster 4) central control plane for rollout and policy, but data plane stays in your VPC.
[10:08] Ravi: any pitfalls we've seen in customers moving to private?
[10:12] Priya: common ones: misconfigured mesh causing long tails, over-aggressive replication saturating peering links, and forgetting to set tenant quotas leading to memory storms. we usually run a capacity plan and network dry-run.
[10:24] Omar: about tooling — can we trigger manual eviction of a tenant during incident?
[10:29] Sofia: yes via the Console you can evict tenant namespace, pin or unpin keys, and set emergency quotas. we log actions for audit.
[10:36] Leah: great. any built-in heuristics for warm-starting caches for new tenants?
[10:40] Ethan: yes warm-start via synthetic prefetch: seed common prefixes learned from other tenants if you opt-in for cross-tenant warming, or seed from a customer-provided hotlist. Hypha should use customer-provided hotlist to avoid leakage.
[10:55] Ravi: ok this was useful. let's move to a short demo of simulated workload results (Ethan).
[11:00] [screen share noise / brief pause]
[11:06] Ethan: so here's a simulated cluster — synthetic 100k tenants, heavy tail 5% hotspots. baseline no isolation p99 is 620ms, after per-tenant reserve + hot-lane p99 drops to 180ms, average mem use increases by 18%.
[11:22] Leah: numbers look encouraging. can you drop a CSV of the node-level metrics?
[11:26] Ethan: yes will attach.
[11:28] Ravi: two final questions — licensing/cost for Dedicated vs Private + support response times.
[11:35] Sofia: Dedicated pricing is usage + reserved capacity; Private is license + deployment support. enterprise support SLA included for both with faster incident response on Private at a premium. I'll send a pricing sketch.
[11:45] Omar: last nit — in our threat model we need the ability to prove no cache leakage for regulatory audit. how do we demonstrate that?
[11:53] Priya: audit features: per-request provenance logs, canonicalization audit trail, per-tenant eviction logs, and cryptographic key custody checks. we can produce an evidence bundle for audits.
[12:06] Ravi: perfect. wrapping up — quick recap and next steps?
[12:10] Sofia: recap: 1) run 24h hotkey sim (Ethan), 2) Hypha share anonymized traces (Ravi), 3) Redwood draft eviction policy and namespace config (Priya), 4) schedule pilot kickoff for Private/VPC networking.
[12:24] Ravi: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[12:27] Leah: thanks!
[12:29] Sofia: bye.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional microphone cut and brief crosstalk, some product names transcribed slightly incorrectly (e.g., "Redwood Privet" instead of Private).

References/links mentioned:
- Synthetic workload template (shared link in chat)
- Hypha anonymized log export (to be shared)
- Redwood Console docs on caching and eviction (redwood.com/docs/cache-evict)

End of transcript.
