Azura weekly POC — unit economics & perf sync

This call had an AE + SE from Redwood (Morgan, Priya). Customer prioritized caching and pilot economics. Several action items assigned. The transcript includes occasional mis-transcriptions (e.g., 'KV cash' for KV cache) typical of Fireflies exports.
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-28
Start: 10:30 AM PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Hale (Azura Product), Miguel Santos (Azura ML Eng), Samir Patel (Azura Infra)
Notes / links: deck: https://drive.link/azura-poc-deck, perf sheet: https://sheets.link/azura-perf, security doc: https://redwood.link/soc2-summary

Summary:
Quick sync on pilot economics — focused on tokens/sec/$ from last week, effect of prefix/KV caching on unit cost, and batching tradeoffs. Decided to run extended dedicated benchmark and capture end-to-end latency under load. Action items and pricing follow.

Topics:
- recent token / second per dollar numbers (week over week)
- observed caching hit rate vs expected
- batching latency tradeoffs for interactive flows
- dedicated pool benchmark plan and instrumentation

Transcript:
00:00 Morgan: okay everybody, uh thanks for carving out time. This is Morgan from Redwood, i'll kick us off. we are at about, what, 48 minutes for the sync. Um Priya's with me from SE and she'll run the perf portion.
00:18 Jordan: hey Morgan, thanks. we've got Samir and Miguel on the Azura side. priority this week is cost signal — we saw an uptick in tokens per dollar on repeat chats.
00:30 Priya: quick note, yesterday's run used the 8-bit quantized variant; that reduced GPU memory and nominal token cost but we saw slightly higher tail latency on long contexts.
00:46 Miguel: yeah i wanted to flag that — when users do long back-and-forths the KV cash — sorry, KV cache — hit rate drops to like 35% on average which spiked token generation time. might be due to our session split logic.
01:05 Samir: and from infra side, we're seeing the burst autoscale fire twice overnight which drove up transient cost. curious if Redwood's routing could fallback to a cheaper variant when capacity's thin.
01:20 Morgan: absolutely, that's part of the routing policy options. we can route to a lower-cost model variant or to region fallback; Priya can talk about policy config.
01:30 Priya: yeah, so there are two knobs that matter: batching window and model variant. For interactive flows we recommend tight batching (20-40ms) to keep latency sub-200ms; for background batched work you can increase batching to 200-400ms and cut tokens/sec/$ cost.
01:55 Jordan: can you give concrete numbers? our PM loop needs a slide — tokens per dollar and the delivered latency.
02:05 Priya: sure. on the hosted baseline with our default gpt-ish open model, last week you saw ~12k tokens / $1 with 90th latency ~240ms. With prefix KV caching enabled we measured effective tokens/$ to ~18k — that was the big delta. On dedicated quantized pool, tokens/$ jumps to ~28k but 99th latency increased by 80-120ms in some traces.
02:38 Miguel: those numbers sound roughly like what we saw. i will say the 18k was when cache hit rate was 62%. when it drops to 35% our observed tokens/$ falls back to around 13k.
02:52 Priya: exactly, so caching amplifies economics strongly but it's brittle to session fragmentation.
03:02 Jordan: ok so we need to know how to keep cache hit rate up. Miguel, is sessionization something we can tune quickly?
03:10 Miguel: yes — we can change our context stitching to keep more of the last N messages in the prefix, but that will increase average input token size which changes batching behavior.
03:22 Samir: and that ties to throughput — bigger inputs mean more decoding time per request; so tokens/sec might drop but tokens/$ could still improve because of fewer redundant generations.
03:36 Morgan: good point. For the pilot we recommended two parallel experiments: 1) increased prefix window to raise caching hit rate and measure tokens/$; 2) dedicated 8-hour steady-state run to measure tokens/sec/$ under representative traffic with the quantized model.
03:54 Jordan: agree. timeline? we need results before the Friday exec sync.
04:02 Morgan: we can get an 8-hour run this week; Priya, can you run it on Thursday?
04:08 Priya: yep Thursday morning. i'll run it on the dedicated pool with the q4 quant build and enable KV cache tracing. will push logs to the perf sheet.
04:18 Miguel: i'll share session traces and current sessionization logic by Wednesday.
04:22 Samir: i'll share VPC peering rules and confirm we can accept Redwood test agents — we prefer to lock down IPs.
04:30 Morgan: perfect. now i'll walk through the perf dashboard quick share — Priya over to you for the numbers walkthrough.
04:38 Priya: slide one is tokens/sec vs latency. we instrument both client and server. an important caveat: our instrumented tokens/sec is normalized for batch size; so when you bump batching window tokens/sec can look better because you're amortizing setup costs.
05:00 Miguel: small note — our user-facing SLA is 300ms typical, 500ms 95th. many of the interactive flows are sensitive above 350ms.
05:12 Priya: right so our recommendation: keep interactive batching window low, enable prefix caching aggressively for interactive, and offload heavy summarization jobs to a background queue with large batching.
05:28 Jordan: what about the autoscale spikes? how can we prevent surprise cost?
05:34 Priya: two things: warm dedicated buffers for expected peak, or configure burst caps and fallback routing. With fallback you can send overflow traffic to a cheaper hosted tier with slightly higher latency but predictable unit cost.
05:50 Samir: would that preserve data residency? we need to ensure overflow doesn't send PII to hosted.
05:56 Morgan: good catch — we can set route filters by dataset tag. Redwood policy allows data-masked or only non-sensitive payloads to go to hosted; anything marked sensitive stays in dedicated.
06:12 Miguel: can we get an estimate for how much overflow would cost relative to dedicated? like tokens/$ delta.
06:19 Priya: rough ballpark: hosted fallback might be ~60% of dedicated tokens/$ (i.e., less efficient), but because it's cheaper per-hour capacity it can flatten overall spend during peaks. we'll quantify in the benchmark.
06:32 Jordan: okay. one other ask — we're running a throughput-critical batch overnight that needs deterministic latency; any thoughts on batching tradeoffs there?
06:42 Priya: for deterministic you should pin to a dedicated pool sized for expected concurrency and configure a small fixed batching window; avoid autoscale during that window or prewarm replicas. Also consider single-request mode on some instances for strict latency.
06:58 Miguel: single-request mode — that'll be more expensive but predictable. for the overnight job we can tolerate higher cost if it's a SLAd batch.
07:06 Samir: on the security side, we're ready to do a short review next week. need the SOC2 summary and audit logs sampling.
07:14 Morgan: i'll send SOC2 summary link after this call (see notes). we can also share truncated audit log samples for your review.
07:22 Jordan: great. back to caching — any tips on designing prompts to increase hit rate?
07:28 Priya: yes: canonicalize system prompts, reduce per-message entropy in non-critical fields, and keep metadata out of the immediate prefix when possible. that helps the cache key match.
07:40 Miguel: that'll require some infra change, but doable. also i want to run an experiment to see if we can batch similar sessions together to improve cache locality.
07:50 Priya: interesting — session affinity grouping can help but might add device affinity complexity; we'll add that to the experiment list.
08:02 Morgan: quick recap: Priya runs 8h dedicated benchmark Thursday, Miguel shares traces Wednesday, Samir confirms peering Monday/Tue, Morgan sends pricing + SOC2 by Friday morning.
08:18 Jordan: sounds good. any open concerns about model quality regressions when quantized?
08:24 Priya: minor risk — we run evals on your prompt set before switching and, if needed, we can pin to a slightly larger fp16 model for specific critical flows. quantization saves cost but comes with small delta in quality for some generation patterns.
08:40 Miguel: please include BLEU/ROUGE-ish diffs as part of the benchmark results for our three sample flows.
08:48 Priya: will do. we'll also include tokenization-level diffs and sample generations at 95th latency points.
08:58 Samir: last infra question — any recommended tracing headers or sampling rates?
09:02 Priya: sample 1% of requests fully, and 100% of 95th+ latency events. include request_id, session_id, and cache_hit boolean.

On-prem VPC setup + latency surgery — Arcadia HealthTech

Deep technical session to diagnose high 99p latency in Arcadia's private VPC deployment. Covered PrivateLink vs TGW routing, split-horizon DNS with on-prem resolvers, NAT design for egress, KV cache warmup/placement, batching tradeoffs, and quantization effects on throughput. Agreed pilot tests and security doc handoff.
PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway routing decisions
DNS resolution and split-horizon approach for on-prem resolvers
Designing NAT/proxy egress (hairpinning, source IP, connection tracking)
KV cache placement, warm starts, and cross-AZ latency
Batching and tokenization interactions with short vs long-tail requests
Quantization tradeoffs: int8 vs fp16 for throughput/latency
Autoscaling behaviors under bursty synchronous traffic
Security controls: KMS, HSM, SSO, audit logs for private deployments
Ravi Menon: Run KV cache cold-start benchmark on Arcadia staging (3 AZs) and share latency histogram by 2026-10-19
Samir Patel: Provide VPC route table + NAT gateway metrics and per-AZ egress stats by 2026-10-14
Tara Singh: Share Redwood Private network runbook and Privatelink config snippets (obfuscated) by 2026-10-13
Maya Lopez: Confirm compliance contact and provide SOC2 scope questions by 2026-10-16
Redwood to send security whitepaper + audit checklist
Schedule 1-hour pilot kickoff for KV cache + batching experiments (week of 10/19)
Customer to open ticket with cloud provider for suspected NAT conntrack saturation
Exchange a small sample of production trace logs (sanitized) for root-cause analysis
[00:00] Jules Carter: Hey everybody, thanks for joining. uh, we got about an hour, and the goal is, uh, to — to go through the networking, the KV cache behaviour, and then layering in batching and quantization, um, to try and find the cause of the 99p spikes you saw.
[00:18] Maya Lopez: Yep thanks Jules. Quick context — we run Redwood Private in our VPC, two compute AZs, a third for standby. Most traffic to the model is internal via privatelink endpoints but some egress goes through a NAT proxy in az-3. We see normal p50 but 99s jump to 2–3s.
[00:36] Ravi Menon: Okay, good. First quick question: when that 99th spike happens, is the traffic pattern short prompts, lots of small requests, or big tokens?
[00:45] Samir Patel: Mostly short prompts, like 10–30 tokens, but bursts of concurrent sessions — chat UI users, and some internal batch jobs at lunchtime that are synchronous.
[00:58] Tara Singh: That's interesting because batching favors long requests for amortization. With short prompts, you can end up with tiny batches which hurts throughput and increases scheduling overhead.
[01:12] Oliver Reed: Also want to note we saw connection resets on the NAT side during peaks, so maybe conntrack or ephemeral port exhaustion.
[01:22] Lina Chen: And from SecOps we saw DNS resolution sometimes goes to the on-prem resolver that has a 200–300ms tail at times. Might be split-horizon configuration.
[01:33] Jules Carter: Cool, thanks. Let's walk through the stack. First, PrivateLink: are you routing via interface endpoints inside the VPC or using TGW and an interconnect?
[01:45] Maya Lopez: We're using interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink style), one per AZ, and we do cross-AZ failover by route tables. There's also a transit VPC that talks to on-prem via a managed VPN.
[01:58] Ravi Menon: Alright. Two immediate flags: (1) cross-AZ failover may cause requests to hit a different AZ if endpoint health checks flip, adding inter-AZ latency; (2) DNS split-horizon — if your resolver sometimes returns the on-prem IP for the endpoint host, traffic could be hairpinned through VPN causing big variance.
[02:18] Samir Patel: So split-horizon could give us the private on-prem endpoint occasionally? Hmm. We do have an internal resolver that forwards unknowns to on-prem.
[02:29] Tara Singh: A common pattern: configure VPC resolver to prefer VPC endpoints and have conditional forwarders for the vendor domain. Otherwise you get intermittent on-prem resolution under load.
[02:41] Jules Carter: Right. Next, NAT and conntrack: Oliver, you mentioned resets — what's the NAT type? Managed NAT Gateway? A NAT instance?
[02:52] Oliver Reed: It's a managed NAT gateway in az-3 and we also have an egress proxy cluster behind a load balancer in the transit VPC. During spikes the NAT's conntrack table hits about 80% of documented limits, then we see resets.
[03:08] Ravi Menon: That would definitely cause tail amplification. NAT conntrack saturation means packets get dropped or reset and TCP handshakes re-try, which adds huge latency at 99p. Two mitigations: increase conntrack / use multiple NAT gateways per AZ, or move egress to a stateful proxy that uses keep-alives from upstream to reduce ephemeral churn.
[03:27] Samir Patel: We also have short TCP timeouts on clients. Could those interplay and increase ephemeral ports usage?
[03:33] Tara Singh: Yes — short client-side timeouts + no connection reuse = more new connections, explosion in conntrack. For LLM serving you want persistent keep-alives and connection pooling.
[03:42] Maya Lopez: For the KV cache — where does Redwood recommend placing it in a private deployment? We currently have the cache in a separate AZ to centralize.
[03:51] Ravi Menon: Centralizing the cache can introduce 1–2x inter-AZ RTT depending on path. For KV cache (prefix/KV), the hotspot is on cache misses — miss latency propagates to generation latency. We recommend placing caches co-located with serving GPU pods per AZ or using a lightweight local L0 cache on the host for the hot working set, then a regional L1 cache.
[04:12] Oliver Reed: We saw a tail where misses to the regional cache added 80–120ms per request at 99p.
[04:18] Ravi Menon: That matches; request path: client -> endpoint -> serving -> check local L0 -> regional L1 -> disk. Every hop adds variance. If you can warm a local L0 with most common prefixes (via pre-warm or on-startup priming) you remove that tail.
[04:33] Samir Patel: How about KV cache replication? We worried about consistency if we replicate across AZs.
[04:40] Tara Singh: For inference it's okay to have eventual consistency; the tradeoff is availability vs strict sync. Use async replication and accept minor staleness — you gain lower read latency.
[04:50] Jules Carter: Let's talk batching: your traffic is short prompts and bursty — Ravi, any config suggestions?
[04:56] Ravi Menon: Sure. Use adaptive batching with a small max latency cap (e.g., 30–40ms) and a burst smoothing window. Also enable prefix caching plus request coalescing on the client side where possible. If the UI is chatty, merge near-simultaneous requests in the browser layer to reduce tiny batches.
[05:14] Maya Lopez: We can change the client — but some third-party apps will still hit the API directly.
[05:19] Tara Singh: In that case, set server-side batching policy conservative: lower max batch size but lower per-request scheduling overhead by keeping worker threads warm and reusing sequence buffers. Also consider batching by token-length histogram — group similar sequence lengths to reduce padding.
[05:33] Samir Patel: Quantization — we tried int8 on one model and saw lower throughput good, but sometimes higher tail latencies. Why?
[05:41] Ravi Menon: Two reasons: (1) quantized kernels can be faster per-token but sometimes have jittery runtimes depending on kernel selection and vectorization; (2) memory layout differences can cause rare page faults if memory wasn't pre-pinned — cold paths show up as tail latency. Solution: warm up quantized kernels and pre-pin memory; use a mixed precision profile for stable latency.
[06:02] Oliver Reed: Do you have tooling to benchmark quantization per workload?
[06:06] Ravi Menon: Yes — we have perf harness scripts that run synthetic token streams and capture kernel latencies and p95/p99. We'll drop that to you.
[06:12] Lina Chen: On the security side, we need to confirm KMS/HSM flow for model keys and whether audit logs include per-request model version.
[06:19] Jules Carter: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS integration and per-request audit logs; we'll include the exact log schema in the security pack.
[06:26] Maya Lopez: Back to DNS — is the recommendation to force VPC resolver to answer the vendor domain locally?
[06:31] Ravi Menon: Yes, conditional forwarding to the vendor endpoints or adding a VPC HOSTS entry for point-in-time will stop on-prem forwarders from handing back on-prem IPs. Also ensure the TTLs are low during rollout.
[06:42] Samir Patel: We saw in traces that sometimes the endpoint IP resolved to an on-prem address for ~5% of requests which matches the 99p spike times.
[06:49] Tara Singh: That's a smoking gun. Fixing split-horizon should immediately drop the 99p from seconds to hundreds of ms.
[06:57] Jules Carter: Let's put together a prioritized mitigation list: 1) Fix DNS split-horizon/conditional forwarding; 2) Reduce NAT conntrack pressure (more NAT gateways or move egress to proxy with keepalives); 3) Local KV L0 caching + priming; 4) Batching tuning + client coalescing; 5) Quantization warmup and mem pinning.
[07:17] Maya Lopez: Sounds good. For the pilot, we want Redwood to help run the KV cold-start test and also validate NAT behaviors if possible.
[07:24] Ravi Menon: We'll run KV cold-start microbenchmarks and synthetic burst tests from your staging AZs. We'll also provide a set of tcpdump and conntrack thresholds to watch for.
[07:33] Oliver Reed: We'll open a cloud ticket after we collect the timestamps and packet counters that Ravi asks for.
[07:39] Lina Chen: One more compliance question: do audit logs include DNS queries or only endpoint accesses?
[07:44] Jules Carter: We capture endpoint-level accesses and trace ids; for raw DNS you'd need to keep resolver logs — Redwood can accept ingest of resolver logs for correlation but we don't store raw DNS by default. We'll document options.
[07:56] Samir Patel: Any recommendation on autoscaling policies to avoid cold start thundering?
[08:01] Tara Singh: Use warm pools and predictive scaling based on usage windows, keep a minimum warm replica per AZ, and prefer scale-in delays to avoid immediate termination during brief lulls.
[08:13] Rav i Menon: sorry Ravi — small mis-s.. (laugh) — and pre-warming with synthetic tokens can keep kernels hot.
[08:18] Maya Lopez: OK good. Could you email the runbook and a short checklist we can hand to infra and sec?
[08:24] Jules Carter: Absolutely. We'll send the network runbook, the KV cache priming script, perf harness, and the security pack.
[08:30] Tara Singh: Also adding a tiny snippet for client coalescing in JS and Go so your front-end teams can implement quick fixes.
[08:37] Maya Lopez: Great. I think that's all for now. Thanks everyone.
[08:40] Jules Carter: We'll follow up with the action items. Thanks all.
[08:44] — end of recording —

Notes on transcription: occasional garble on product names (privatelink sometimes transcribed 'private link' or 'privatelinc'); timings approximate; speakers labeled by meeting roster where possible.

NexaHealth pilot — latency metrics review & inference pathing decisions

Weekly POC sync focused on reducing TTFT and stabilizing streaming latency. Reviewed recent runs: hosted baseline, dedicated with fused kernels, and a quantized 4-bit variant. Identified two clear experiments: kernel A/B across real prompts and streaming chunk-size tuning in client infra. Agreed on data handoffs and dates for next steps.
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick agenda — quick status, results we shipped this week, Carlos will go through the kernel numbers, then we want to decide next experiments for the pilot.
[00:25] Priya (NexaHealth - ML): Thanks. we've been seeing some variability in start-up latency, TTFT is kinda all over when we hit long inputs.
[00:40] Carlos (Redwood SE): Cool, I'll try to be succinct. baseline hosted run — with the default runtime and no prefix cache — TTFT median about 120ms, p95 210ms on your typical 256 token prompt set. After we enabled fused-attn kernels and tuned the scheduler we saw median drop to ~78ms p95 140ms, but that was on our dedicated infra trace.
[01:15] David (NexaHealth - Infra): Is that with batching? we usually have bursts that push up queueing.
[01:25] Carlos: These numbers were single request paths, minimal batching to measure TTFT. We also did small-batch tests (batch size 4) where avg per-token latency was slightly better for throughput but TTFT increased by ~20ms because of the batching window.
[01:45] Priya: Right, so for our real-time summarization flow TTFT matters more than token cost.
[01:52] Maya: Totally, that was our assumption. so we need the model path that favors TTFT — lower startup overhead — while keeping streaming smooth.
[02:05] Carlos: We also looked at quantization. 4-bit qform gave a small TTFT improvement (about 8-12ms) but the variance increased on corner cases — long sequences. Might be quantization noise or different kernel fallback.
[02:26] Sara (Product): Are there quality regressions when you quantize? we can't degrade extractive summarization metrics.
[02:33] Carlos: We ran the eval harness on your eval set — Rouge/F1 dropped <0.6% on average but a few outliers at the long end did show slight hallucination flags, so we flagged those prompts.
[02:50] Priya: okay please mark those outliers. we can consider a hybrid approach — quantized for short flows, full precision for long.
[02:58] Carlos: Exactly. that's one of the options.
[03:05] Maya: Quick note — shared the benchmark sheet earlier (link: https://redwood.share/bench/nexa-aug) — folks should be able to view.
[03:16] David: got it. saw the kernel runs, curious about streaming chunking — how big were the chunks you tested?
[03:24] Carlos: We tried 64 token chunks and 128 token chunks. 64 gave lower per-chunk latency but more HTTP overhead; 128 fewer chunks but slightly higher latency for early tokens. For TTFT + perceived start, 64 felt snappier.
[03:40] Priya: our UX team suggested showing first sentence within 150ms ideally. Are we close?
[03:46] Carlos: With fused kernels + 64-token streaming and little to no batching, median first-byte ~85ms on dedicated; hosted was around 120ms depending on region egress.
[04:02] Priya: That aligns with what we saw. the problem is in staging sometimes it jumps to 300ms at p95.
[04:10] Carlos: Those spikes matched times when KV cache misses happened; one of your longer prompts warmed up different KV table shapes. our suggestion: prefix caching for repeated conversation IDs + small warm-up trick.
[04:24] David: how intrusive is prefix caching to our infra? we've got strict mem budgets.
[04:30] Carlos: It's a runtime-side optimization; for dedicated we can tune cache size. For hosted you'd rely on our adaptive eviction. Memory impact is proportional to cached kv size and sequence length; we can show expected mem curves in the bench sheet.
[04:43] Maya: we'll add mem curve plots to the sheet.
[04:47] Sara: What about kernel selection? you mentioned fused-attn — any other kernels?
[04:51] Carlos: There's fused-attn (good for short-medium seq), block-sparse kernels for very long sequences, and a fallback vectorized kernel. The tradeoffs are latency vs throughput and stability. The A/B we want to run is fused-attn vs default optimized vector kernel across your live prompt distribution.
[05:12] Priya: That distribution includes some ~2k token prompts for research summaries — do fused-attn handle that?
[05:18] Carlos: Fused-attn degrades as seq grows; block-sparse or chunked attention works better beyond ~1k tokens. That's why we asked for the histogram of your prompt lengths.
[05:30] Priya: I'll upload that.
[05:33] Maya: Reminder: action item for Priya to send 200 long-tail prompts and histogram.
[05:38] [06:00] Carlos: Quick note on network: when we saw p95 spikes in hosted tests some were due to edge egress limits in your VPC setup — David, you mentioned your router caps were 500 rps?
[06:12] David: yes, burst to 750 in peak, but sustained is 500.
[06:17] Carlos: For the streaming experiment we'll need a test window where you lift egress capping to reproduce the bursts; otherwise the network masks runtime gains.
[06:24] David: okay we can do a scheduled window.
[06:28] [07:00] Priya: let's talk instrumentation — we'd like token-level latencies in our APM. can you provide trace hooks?
[07:08] Maya: yes, the SDK emits token-level events and trace IDs; we can drop a tracing example into the shared repo.
[07:14] Carlos: We'll also include a micro-benchmark script you can run behind your router to simulate sustained bursts and streaming chunking.
[07:22] Priya: great.
[07:25] [09:00] Sara: so decision point — do we prioritize fused-attn (low TTFT for most traffic) or hybrid with dynamic kernel selection?
[09:10] Carlos: Our recommendation is dynamic routing: fused-attn for <512 tokens, block-sparse or chunked for >1k, and a fallback to vectorized when we detect instability. But dynamic adds complexity.
[09:25] Priya: complexity is okay if ops overhead is low. we can't have more than 1% error budget.
[09:31] Maya: Also reminded that Dedicated gives us more levers (cache size, kernel tuning) while hosted is faster to iterate.
[09:40] David: Are there cost numbers? switching to dedicated for this pilot impacts spend.
[09:45] Maya: Carlos, quick cost delta?
[09:48] Carlos: Dedicated pilot estimated +25% monthly cost but gives steady p99 and lower TTFT variance. The merged savings from quantization and batching could offset 10-12% depending on traffic shape. We'll put a cost scenario table in the sheet.
[10:08] [12:00] Priya: I'm concerned about quality with quantization — can we do a guardrail that routes prompts above N tokens to full precision automatically?
[12:12] Carlos: Yes, can be policy-based routing — sequence-length threshold triggers full-precision instance. It's part of the rollout config.
[12:20] Priya: ok do that for now.
[12:22] [14:00] Maya: Quick pause — any blockers from legal/security?
[14:07] Sara: We need the SOC 2 attestation and a copy of audit log format; you shared earlier but need example entries.
[14:15] Maya: I'll resend the SOC2 PDF and an example of the audit log lines. 
[14:21] [16:00] David: For the streaming trial we need your sample client that uses keepalive and small chunk windows — can you provide?
[16:07] Carlos: Yes, we have a streaming client repo; will handover link and a dockerized example.
[16:15] Maya: I'll add that to the bench sheet links.
[16:20] [18:00] Priya: Let's set measurable success criteria for the next run — target median TTFT <100ms, p95 <160ms on our primary region for 95% of test set. If we hit those we expand the pilot.
[18:32] Carlos: Accepted, we'll try to hit those in the A/B kernel run.
[18:38] [20:00] Sara: Also want an explicit rollback plan if quality dips with quantization.
[20:06] Maya: policy-based routing plus canary on small % traffic is the plan, with auto-fallback to full precision model. We'll document steps.
[20:18] [22:00] Carlos: Technical detail — when you stream with 64 token chunks we recommend small TCP keepalive of 15s and client ack windows to avoid connection resets. Otherwise we saw a chunk lost behavior and re-sends that add ~120ms.
[22:36] David: noted. we'll adjust infra.
[22:40] [25:00] Priya: Any surprises in the data?
[25:06] Carlos: One thing — a small subset of prompts triggered a kernel fallback in runtime because of certain attention mask patterns; that added 200-300ms. We're flagging those prompts and will include mask-normalization in the preproc suggestions.
[25:22] Priya: we'll test normalization.
[25:26] [28:00] Maya: Recap time — Carlos will run kernel A/B (fused vs default) on 1k prompt set, include mem curves, quality diffs and upload to bench by 26th. Priya will send long-tail prompts and histogram by 22nd. David will open a scheduled egress window and send router config. Maya will send SOC2 + audit log example and pricing doc by tomorrow.
[28:58] Sara: can we also get a short doc on rollback and canary config?
[29:05] Maya: yes, will add a one-pager.
[29:14] [32:00] Priya: how about timeline — after the kernel A/B, when do we reconvene?
[32:08] Maya: propose 2025-08-28 for a streaming deep-dive with your infra team.
[32:15] Priya: works for us.
[32:18] [35:00] Carlos: small note on metrics — please enable token-level tracing and include trace IDs with bench runs so we can map spikes to kernel choices.
[35:12] David: will do.
[35:16] [38:00] Sara: any competitor comments — we had an RFP and MegaCloud AI offered a lower cost but higher TTFT; we prefer Redwood's tunability.
[38:10] Maya: good to know — we'll highlight cost vs latency tradeoffs in the scenario table.
[38:20] [42:00] Priya: final question — if fused-attn gives best TTFT for 70% of traffic but struggles on 5% extremes, will Redwood's runtime auto-fallback be seamless?
[42:12] Carlos: Yes, the runtime supports hot fallback; the initial hit is a small latency bump while the alternative kernel spins up, usually <200-300ms on those single occurrences.
[42:24] Priya: ok acceptable if infrequent.
[42:30] [45:00] Maya: okay folks, thanks — we'll track action items in the bench sheet and update next steps. next call 2025-08-28 for the streaming deep dive.

[45:20] David: thanks.

Semantics & Rerank Integration - Discovery

Initial discovery for embeddings and rerank integration. Atlas is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private for latency-sensitive product search. Key concerns: embedding dimensionality, rerank latency, vector DB choice, hybrid recall, security (VPC, KMS), and predictable throughput for peak retail traffic.
Meeting header
Date: 2025-10-22
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Tom Hsu (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Atlas Head of Search), Rahul Singh (Atlas ML Lead), Ben Carter (Atlas Eng Manager)

Summary: (auto) Atlas is considering Redwood for semantic search + reranking for ecommerce product search. Needs to understand latency, throughput, and infra patterns.

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — I'm Maya, AE at Redwood. Tom's our SE. How are you all?
[00:08] Lena Ortiz: Hey Maya, hi Tom. Doing well. Excited to chat. We have a lot of questions around embeddings and rerank throughput.
[00:14] Tom Hsu: Great. I'll try to cover the architecture tradeoffs and then we can dig into the benchmarks you need.
[00:22] Rahul Singh: Our main product is search for fashion catalog. Peak QPS during drops is really spiky like 3k qps for short windows. We need sub-200ms median for initial recall and sub-400ms for final ranked results ideally.
[00:35] Ben Carter: And we have strict data residency — all user data stays in our VPC. So Private or Dedicated are the likely options, but cost is also a concern.
[00:45] Maya Patel: Understood. Can you share current stack? Are you using an embedding store today?
[00:51] Lena Ortiz: We're currently on Elastic + a small FAISS cluster for semantic recall. FAISS is self-hosted on k8s, but it's brittle at scale and our cross-encoder rerank runs on CPU which kills latency.
[01:05] Tom Hsu: Okay so common pattern: bi-encoder for candidate retrieval, then cross-encoder for re-ranking. Do you run your cross-encoder as part of the retrieval path or asynchronously?
[01:14] Rahul Singh: Sync, because we need re-ranking for personalization and exact ordering. So latency budget is tight.
[01:21] Tom Hsu: For that pattern, two knobs matter: embedding dimensionality and vector DB latency for kNN. Higher dim (1536) gives better recall usually but costs more CPU/GPU and storage. Lower dim (512) runs faster and is cheaper but may lose niche queries.
[01:38] Lena Ortiz: We saw 768->1536 jumps helped recall on long descriptions but our cost doubled. Curious how Redwood recommends balancing that.
[01:46] Maya Patel: Redwood typically suggests starting with the smallest dim that meets your recall on a representative eval set. For retail catalogs, 512 or 768 often suffices; 1536 reserved for multimodal or long text. Tom, maybe note the eval suggestion?
[01:58] Tom Hsu: Yep. We'll run an A/B with 512 vs 1536 on your sample set. Also important is vector index type — flat vs HNSW vs IVF. HNSW is great for latency at scale but memory-heavy. IVF PQ helps with storage but has recall tradeoffs and slower second-stage checks.
[02:18] Rahul Singh: On the vendor side, we're eyeing Pinecone for ease, but worried about egress and cost. Also want the ability to run on-prem later.
[02:27] Maya Patel: That maps to Redwood Dedicated or Private: Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity in our infra; Private sits in your VPC or on-prem with our control plane. We can support the same API surface for all three.
[02:40] Ben Carter: For Private, do you support KMS or HSM for key management? And audit logs?
[02:45] Tom Hsu: Yes — KMS integrations are available, HSM is possible via partners. Audit logs and fine-grained RBAC are standard in Private. We'll attach the security pack.
[02:55] Lena Ortiz: How about rerank model serving? We're currently running a cross-encoder (distil-bert based) that takes ~120ms per request on our CPU nodes which is too slow. If we move to GPU, what throughput can we expect?
03:08 Rahul Singh (transcription glitch: 3:08): "+ we run batch sizes of one mostly, sometimes 8."
[03:15] Tom Hsu: On GPU with optimized kernels we can get ~200-500 QPS for a small distil cross-encoder depending on batch sizing and token lengths, P99 varies. For large cross-encoders it drops. Key trick is batching and async prefix caching for the bi-encoder.
[03:32] Maya Patel: We have a quantized pathway that can lower memory and cost; Redwood Optimize can suggest per-model quantization and batch configs. But the rerank cross-encoder often needs full precision for quality-sensitive ranking.
[03:45] Ben Carter: So practically speaking, if we wanted to hold 3k spike QPS, do you recommend dedicated pool or hybrid route where Redwood hosts the cross-encoder and our FAISS stays in our VPC?
[03:57] Tom Hsu: A hybrid is common: host cross-encoder on Dedicated GPUs (or Private) and keep vector index where you want. We support remote vector DB connections — Redwood can read from your FAISS or from hosted index with secure plumbing (VPC peering or private link). For spikes you can configure burst capacity.
[04:19] Rahul Singh: Can you talk about latency numbers end-to-end for a hybrid path — say 512 dim, HNSW, topK 100, then cross-encoder rerank top 10?
[04:28] Tom Hsu: Rough numbers: Vector retrieval (HNSW) on optimized index ~20-50ms, network adds 10-30ms depending on metal. Cross-encoder per-item 10-30ms on GPU in batch; so reranking top10 at batch size 10 could be ~50-120ms. So end-to-end ~100-220ms typical if everything is colocated; if indices remote add some tail latency.
[04:52] Lena Ortiz: That sounds promising. Our requirement of <400ms final seems doable. Cost question: do you meter per-token for rerank when using Redwood hosted cross-encoder?
[05:02] Maya Patel: For hosted API we meter per-token; for Dedicated/Private it's capacity-based. We can show a cost model: per-request compute cost + vector DB storage cost. We'll include example numbers based on your sample.
[05:14] Ben Carter: We care about determinism and cold-starts. Do you implement KV cache for generation? Not sure if applies to rerank but for other parts of pipeline it matters.
[05:23] Tom Hsu: KV cache is primarily for autoregressive generation; for rerank it's less relevant. For cross-encoders caching of features or precomputed embeddings for candidates can help; we also support prefix caching at the bi-encoder level.
[05:38] Rahul Singh: For the index migration, we have about 50k products but we project 2M in 12 months. Any guidance on index management and sharding?
[05:47] Tom Hsu: For that growth plan, I recommend HNSW with sharded partitions. Redwood Dedicated supports sharding and autoscaling. For private, you can set similar policies; we can help design the partition strategy so re-balancing isn't painful.
[06:02] Maya Patel: Quick question — are there regulatory constraints e.g., EU data staying in region?
[06:06] Lena Ortiz: Yes EU customer data must stay in EU for some countries. We need region controls.

Handoff meeting between Redwood AE/SE and ArborCore procurement/legal to align on MSA/DPA redlines, SLA expectations, pricing variance, and next steps for a pilot. Key open items: DPA redlines, pricing sheet, 24-hour benchmark data, and procurement timeline. Decision leaning toward Dedicated pool with private VPC but final depends on egress/latency benchmarks and DPA changes.
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-08
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~47 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Rajiv Kapoor (ArborCore - Head of Platform), Lena Ortiz (ArborCore - Counsel), Tom Brooks (ArborCore - Procurement), Simone Park (ArborCore - Security)

Auto-summary (may be rough): Handing off commercial and legal conversation; quick technical validation plan; identify DPA redlines and procurement path.

00:00:05 Avery (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. we'll try to be concise — this is the procurement/legal handover after our technical eval last week, so Maya and I will run through the commercial bits, legal asks, and proposed pilot plan.
00:00:18 Rajiv: Yep thanks, we want to make sure the procurement team and counsel are aligned. we've got some internal deadlines — finance wants a procurement decision window by end of month, so timelines matter.
00:00:30 Lena: Hi all. quick note from legal: we'll share redlines to the DPA and MSA. primary concerns are data residency for PII-derived artifacts, audit log retention, and privileged access.
00:00:45 Maya (Redwood SE): Great, thanks Lena. On the technical side our suggestion based on the benchmark was Dedicated capacity in a private VPC if you need deterministic latency and isolation; Hosted is cheaper for bursty dev work but doesn't meet the isolation we're hearing.
00:01:02 Tom: When you say "Dedicated," does that imply a reserved commit and a monthly fee? how flexible is burst capacity?
00:01:10 Avery: Yes, Dedicated is reserved GPU pools — monthly/annual commits. We offer configurable burst policies so you can have a baseline commit with throttled burst to handle spikes. billing is split: base commit + overage at a discounted rate.
00:01:27 Rajiv: And what about rollback and availability? our SREs care about safe rollouts.
00:01:34 Maya: We support canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a lighter model if a rollout violates latency or error thresholds. We can include that language in the SLA: e.g., canary performance checks and automatic fallback to a previous pinned model version.
00:01:50 Simone (Security): KMS question — can you support customer-managed keys (bring-your-own-key) in Private? and how are keys managed in Dedicated?
00:01:59 Maya: For Private you can use your KMS/HSM and Redwood can integrate for encryption at rest; in Dedicated we support KMS integration via our key leasing flows but root key is still in the cloud provider KMS unless you opt for the Private on-prem package. There may be additional costs for HSM-backed keying.
00:02:18 Lena: On the DPA, we will push for stricter data deletion timelines and a carve-out around model weights if customer data might influence models. we need a clear statement about training / fine-tuning prohibition.
00:02:34 Avery: Redwood's default is no customer data used for model training unless explicitly opted-in. we'll add a clause and an attestation. we can commit to data purge timelines for requestable datasets and to provide audit logs for deletions.
00:02:48 Tom: Egress fees — our finance team flags egress from hosted services. how predictable are those and can you show a cost estimate for our expected token volumes?
00:02:58 Maya: We'll produce per-token cost estimates for fp16, int8 quantized variants and show egress sizing. Dedicated reduces per-token compute but you still have egress/transfer costs if using hosted endpoints. For Private on-prem, egress is internal so different.
00:03:15 Rajiv: We need a 24-hour benchmark run on our sample workload that shows p95 and cost per 1M tokens. can you do that?
00:03:22 Maya: Yes, we'll run a 24-hour benchmark using your sample prompt set and the two model variants we discussed. we'll include latency histograms, token breakdown and cost projection.
00:03:34 Lena: Legal also needs to see SOC2 artifacts and our standard audit checklist before procurement signs off.
00:03:40 Avery: Understood. we'll push SOC2 Type II report and an artifacts pack; if additional evidence needed our compliance team will coordinate.
00:03:50 Tom: Timeline question again — procurement needs to know how soon we can get to a pilot contract after DPA signoff. typical PO cycle is 2–3 weeks after contract approval.
00:03:59 Avery: On Redwood's side, once the MSA/DPA are agreed we can stand up a pilot in dedicated within 5 business days, assuming we have required network access and keys.
00:04:10 Rajiv: Network access — we'll need to share VPC peering details and egress ACLs. Simone will own that.
00:04:17 Simone: yes i'll share topology docs, but we also need to understand what level of telemetry Redwood retains for debugging — logs, KV cache snapshots etc — so we can scope retention in the DPA.
00:04:28 Maya: We retain request logs for troubleshooting by default; KV cache is ephemeral per session but we can configure retention windows. We'll document what is stored and offer options for tighter retention in Private.
00:04:40 Lena: Also want clarity on incident notification timelines and RTO — legal will want those in the SLA.
00:04:47 Avery: We typically commit to incident notification within X hours and a defined escalation ladder; we can map that into SLA and offer a runbook excerpt. for Dedicated we can discuss harder uptime commitments with credits.
00:05:05 Tom: Can you provide sample SLA credit language? finance will want to see downside protections.
00:05:11 Avery: yes i'll include a templated SLA credit schedule and an example for p95 latency breaches and availability.
00:05:18 Rajiv: On pricing, one of our constraints is finops wants predictable unit costs under our commit. do you offer graduated discounts by commit tier?
00:05:26 Maya: yes, committed reserved capacity has tiered discounts. we can model scenarios: small commit with moderate discount vs larger commit with deeper discount. We'll include a blended per-token number for your workload.
00:05:39 Simone: Any third-party subprocessors? who are datacenter providers and will they be named?
00:05:44 Avery: We'll provide a subprocessors list. we work with major cloud providers in-region; if you need named regions we can document that.
00:05:53 Lena: DPA redlines will include data residency and export controls. if your subprocessors include non-EU data centers, that could be an issue for us.
00:06:01 Avery: We can commit to EU-only regions for your tenant for Hosted/Dedicated if that helps. Private on-prem avoids the problem.
00:06:09 Rajiv: Let's talk about evaluation acceptance criteria — what's the bar to move from pilot to production?
00:06:15 Maya: From our side: 1) p95 latency meets your SLOs for 48/72-hour run, 2) error rates below X%, 3) cost per 1M tokens within the agreed threshold, and 4) DPA/MSA accepted. once those are met procurement can move to PO.
00:06:33 Tom: That's helpful. our internal success criteria will mirror that.
00:06:38 Lena: We'll also need a clause on data deletion verification and audit rights.
00:06:43 Avery: We'll produce a deletion attestation flow and can include an audit access schedule.
00:06:49 Rajiv: Quick question on model variants: if we need quantized models for cost reasons, will Redwood manage quantized builds or do we need to provide them?
00:06:58 Maya: Redwood can supply quantized variants and we can recommend quantization profiles. for Dedicated we can also provide precompiled kernels to optimize throughput.
00:07:08 Simone: One more security ask — can we restrict API access by CIDR ranges and enable SSO/SCIM provisioning?
00:07:15 Avery: Yes, we support CIDR restrictions, SAML SSO, and SCIM provisioning for enterprise accounts.
00:07:21 Tom: Any escrow or escrow-equivalent for model weights or business continuity? finance occasionally asks.
00:07:27 Avery: We have escrow options for critical contracts; we'll provide details if needed.
00:07:33 Lena: Ok, i'll send DPA redlines post-call and flag the critical items.
00:07:38 Avery: Great. To recap — action items: we'll run the benchmark, share pricing and SLA templates, provide SOC2 and subprocessors list; you will share DPA redlines and procurement timing.
00:07:52 Rajiv: sounds good. one small nit in the tech notes: is the KV cache snapshot stored anywhere persistent that could leak PII?
00:08:01 Maya: KV cache is in-memory and ephemeral per inference session; we do have optional snapshotting for debugging, but that's off by default and would be part of the pilot configuration.
00:08:12 Tom: Procurement note — our PO requires an approved invoice path and milestone for pilot acceptance. can you support invoicing for a pilot month with a credit term?
00:08:21 Avery: yes, we can do a pilot invoice; payment terms can be discussed with finance.
00:08:26 Rajiv: Any performance regressions with fallbacks? example: if you fallback to a smaller model, how much quality delta should we expect and who owns regression monitoring?
00:08:36 Maya: Quality delta depends on the model family; we'll provide sample BLEU/ROUGE-ish metrics per variant on the 24-hour run. Redwood offers regression monitoring tools but we recommend a joint eval suite to track quality metrics; we can integrate that into Redwood Optimize.
00:08:54 Lena: We'll need an explicit non-retraining clause in the MSA saying Redwood won't use customer prompts for improving models without opt-in.
00:09:01 Avery: we'll include that and provide an attestation.
00:09:06 Rajiv: ok, time check — we have about 35 minutes left but i think the major lines are clear. any final commercial clarifications?
00:09:15 Tom: just define what "burst" costs would look like for our forecast periods.
00:09:20 Maya: We'll add a burst-overage example to the pricing sheet with a worked example for your volume.
00:09:27 Simone: security will follow up on VPC peering specifics, egress ACLs, and KMS flows.
00:09:33 Avery: got it — simone and maya to sync offline on network ops.
00:09:38 (overlap)
00:09:40 Avery: final recap and ask — can lena send the DPA redlines today or tomorrow, that would help accelerate the procurement window?
00:09:47 Lena: yes i'll aim to send a redline bundle by tomorrow EOD.
00:09:52 Rajiv: and maya will run the 24-hour benchmark starting tomorrow?
00:09:56 Maya: yes we'll kick it off tomorrow pending the sample dataset and any network creds.
00:10:02 Tom: procurement will draft a preferred PO template and circulate to avery.
00:10:07 Avery: Great. thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts pack and the pricing sheet.
00:10:12 [call continues with logistics and small clarifications until 15:47 UTC]

Call end remarks:
Avery: appreciate the time. we'll get the benchmark results and pricing model across, and coordinate legal threads. please ping if any blockers.
Lena: thanks, will send redlines.

2025-04-10 POC scoping — reserved GPUs, autoscale & fallback (Kumo Analytics)

Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-10
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Rina Gomez (Redwood CSM); Mike Chen (Kumo ML Lead), Aisha Rahman (Kumo Platform), Carlos Vega (CTO), Lena Ortiz (Product)

Summary: Quick POC scoping to align success criteria, capacity sizing, reserved GPU requirements, burst strategy, and fallback policies. Kumo wants a 4-week pilot to validate 99th percentile latency under load and cost/throughput tradeoffs. Discussed benchmarks, trace capture, autoscale boundaries, and governance (KMS, VPC, SOC2).

Topics: capacity sizing, reserved capacity vs burst, canary/fallback policies, metrics to capture for success, timeline and benchmark window, security requirements

[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, then goal — scope a POC for your inference workload, focused on capacity sizing and autoscale behaviors. Mike, do you want to kick off with current stack?
[00:12] Mike (Kumo): Sure — uh, we run a mixture of single-turn generation and a smaller percentage of multi-turn chat, mostly using an open 7B variant on our own infra. Latency targets are, like, 95th under 180ms for the chat stuff, and avg generation for single-turn around 90ms. We're seeing spikes during product launches, sometimes 3x baseline QPS.
[00:34] Aisha (Platform): Our current infra is kubernetes in GCP, we have a GPU pool but frankly we don't have great burst capacity, that's why we're exploring Redwood dedicated + burst. We need to understand how reserved GPUs work and what the fallback behavior is if the burst capacity is exhausted.
[00:48] Samir (SE): Great context. Two quick clarifications — when you say spikes 3x, is that sustained for minutes or seconds? And do you have p99 SLOs or p95?
[00:59] Mike (Kumo): Usually minutes, 5–15 minutes during a campaign. For this POC we want to validate p99 under load and cost per 1k requests.
[01:12] Jordan (AE): Good. We'll propose reserved capacity for steady-state plus a burst pool for transient spikes. For safety we can set a fallback policy to a cheaper model variant or route to a queued mode — we'll lay options out.
[01:26] Carlos (CTO): I want to be explicit: if burst is used and costs spike, we need a budget cap and alerting. Also, fallback must preserve user experience — immediate degrade to a smaller model is OK but must be labeled.
[01:41] Samir (SE): Noted. For the POC we'll test three modes: 1) reserved-only, 2) reserved + burst with auto-provisioned GPUs, 3) reserved + burst with fallback to a quantized 4-bit variant. We'll capture latency distribution, throughput, and token cost.

[01:58] (Speaker 1): mhmm, and how do you measure tokens?
[02:03] Jordan (AE): We'll align on token accounting in the POC doc. Also we'll need sample prompts and traces. Aisha, you said you could export traces?
[02:11] Aisha (Platform): Yeah I can export, we have Nyx logging, I'll scrub PII, but note some tokens include user metadata.
[02:22] Lena (Product): From product side, success = 99th percentile latency < 250ms for chat flows and cost per 1k under $X (we'll fill). We also want no more than 2% degraded outputs during spikes.

[02:40] Samir (SE): Perfect — that gives us measurable criteria. For capacity sizing we usually take steady-state peak QPS and multiply by concurrency factor and average model latency to back into GPU seconds. We'll run initial guesses today but need traces to do real sizing.
[03:01] Mike (Kumo): Example — baseline 200 RPS, spikes to 600 for 10 minutes, average sequence length ~120 tokens, model latency on our 7B is ~80ms per token? sorry per request? (laugh) It's a bit fuzzy.
[03:18] Samir (SE): No worries; we'll parse traces. Two approaches for the POC: reserve N GPUs to cover baseline headroom and configure burst capacity for the 3x spike. Burst can be instant if we pre-warm containers or slower if we need to spin up. Pre-warm reduces cold-start but costs more.
[03:36] Jordan (AE): Operationally, Redwood Dedicated offers reserved pools (monthly commit) and an optional burst pool billed per-use. For POC we can allocate small reserved capacity and enable a controlled burst budget. If burst budget hits cap, policy options: a) throttle traffic b) route to smaller model variant c) queue requests with a best-effort TTL.
[03:57] Carlos (CTO): Option b seems attractive but we need safeguards around hallucination / quality regression. Is there an automated A/B or canary path?
[04:10] Samir (SE): We support canary rollouts and automatic fallback. For the POC we'll configure canary with a 10% traffic test and look at hallucination metrics via our evals. We'll also set rollback triggers on quality regressions.
[04:25] Mike (Kumo): On monitoring, what telemetry will we get? Token cost, GPU utilization, queue depth?
[04:32] Rina (CSM): Redwood Console will show per-route cost, token breakdown, latency percentiles, GPU utilization, and tracing hooks. We can also forward logs to your Splunk/Datadog.
[04:45] (Speaker 2): Are there limits on burst GPUs per region?
[04:48] Samir (SE): There are practical limits based on our capacity pool and region. For POC we can reserve a guaranteed buffer in the target region to simulate production. If you need multi-region we can test failover too.

[05:05] Mike (Kumo): Let's talk benchmarks — we want to run two windows: a functional run (low QPS) and a sustained stress window with synthetic spikes. Ideally the stress window mirrors real trace shapes.
[05:17] Samir (SE): Agreed. We'll provide a benchmark harness that can replay traces and also a synthetic driver to hit target RPS. We'll also capture p50/p95/p99 and tail latencies during cold starts.
[05:29] Aisha (Platform): Cold start numbers matter; our concern is spin-up time if burst creates new nodes. How long are cold starts?
[05:36] Samir (SE): With pre-warmed containers and warm KV cache, cold starts are sub-10s in many cases; cold starts to fully initialize a model can be 30–90s unless we use snapshot resume or cache warmers. There's also a tradeoff with quantization: smaller models load faster.
[05:55] Jordan (AE): We'll include a warm policy for the POC: keep X pre-warmed replicas to cover base bursts and then scale additional nodes with a target spin-up target. We'll show cost math so Kumo can choose pre-warm vs risk of cold starts.

[06:12] (Speaker 3): What's KV cash?
[06:15] Samir (SE): kv cash — KV cache, sorry — the key-value cache for autoregressive decoding. If KV is warmed the p99 is much better. Our runtime can persist KV cache across requests when it's safe.
[06:28] Mike (Kumo): Any integration work for VPC / private deployment for the POC? We prefer VPC peering for data control.
[06:35] Jordan (AE): For the POC we can do Redwood Dedicated in your VPC with private endpoints. That requires some network setup: peering, firewall rules, and if you want on-prem there is extra packaging. For the short pilot VPC peering is usually sufficient.

[06:49] Carlos (CTO): Security — KMS, audit logs, SOC2 — we need to see proof.
[06:54] Rina (CSM): I'll share SOC2 report, the security whitepaper, and KMS integration notes after the call. We'll also note SAML/SSO support for RBAC.
[07:05] Lena (Product): For success criteria, product also wants an AB test where 10% of live traffic goes through Redwood during the pilot. Can Redwood handle a hybrid routing with split traffic?
[07:15] Samir (SE): Yes — split routing and percent rollouts are supported. We recommend starting with synthetic bench then a canary with real traffic.

[07:23] Jordan (AE): Ok let's walk through an initial sizing example — Samir?
[07:28] Samir (SE): Sure. If baseline is 200 RPS, and average request requires 50ms GPU time, that's 10 GPU-seconds per second, so a single A100 (or equivalent) can handle X concurrently depending on batch efficiency. But the real number depends on sequence length, batching and kv cache hit rate. I'm simplifying.
[07:50] Mike (Kumo): Sorry can you restate GPU-seconds?
[07:53] Samir (SE): GPU-seconds is the cumulative GPU compute per second. If each request occupies the GPU for 50ms, then 20 requests/sec == 1 GPU second per second. So we translate that to number of GPUs needed.
[08:05] Aisha (Platform): Do you recommend fixed concurrency limits per model?
[08:08] Samir (SE): Yes — set a max concurrency per replica to avoid OOM and to keep predictability. We will propose defaults for your model architecture.

[08:20] (Speaker 1): And what about cost accounting for burst — per-minute billing?
[08:24] Jordan (AE): Burst is billed based on GPU-minutes consumed above reserved baseline; we'll provide an estimated cost curve in the proposal. For POC we'll also provide a not-to-exceed budget envelope to keep surprises small.
[08:36] Carlos (CTO): Important: fallback decision tree should be explicit: prefer smaller model variant first, then queue, then degrade. Also need a kill-switch for ops.
[08:47] Samir (SE): We'll include a policy matrix: thresholds on GPU utilization, queue depth, and burst spend — each mapped to an action. For example: if burst spend > $Y or GPU util > 90% for 2 minutes -> route 25% to smaller model, if persists route 50%, eventually queue with 10s TTL.

[09:10] Mike (Kumo): How do we detect quality regression fast enough to rollback?
[09:14] Samir (SE): We'll run lightweight evals on sampled responses — metrics like hallucination score, BLEU-ish similarity to reference, or embedding-distance to golden responses. If metric drift crosses threshold, canary rollback triggers. We'll instrument those in the POC harness.
[09:31] Lena (Product): Are there tooling limits for offline evals?
[09:34] Samir (SE): We can integrate your existing evals or run Redwood's quick eval suite. For POC we recommend a small set of golden prompts.

[09:45] Jordan (AE): Let's capture the POC timeline: week 0 (this week) align on traces & success criteria; week 1 deploy reserved baseline & run small functional tests; week 2 run stress benchmarks and tune pre-warm; week 3 run live canary with 10% of traffic; week 4 collect results and decision (go/no-go). Does that map to your expectations?
[10:08] Carlos (CTO): That seems fine. We have a product launch at the end of May so tight but doable.
[10:15] Aisha (Platform): For the benchmark run we'll need credentials & sandbox. What access do you need?
[10:20] Samir (SE): We'll need API keys for a sandbox project, sample prompts, and traces. For VPC peering we'll need IP ranges and firewall contact.

[10:32] (Speaker 2): On quantization — you mentioned 4-bit. Does Redwood support int4 runtime?
[10:36] Samir (SE): Yes, we support several quantized runtimes including 4-bit and 8-bit paths. For some models int4 reduces quality slightly but speeds and memory usage improve dramatically. We'll include a quantization recommendation per model in the POC.
[10:49] Mike (Kumo): Any sample numbers on throughput improvements?
[10:52] Samir (SE): Typically 1.5–3x throughput improvement depending on the model and ops. We'll quantify for your exact model in the benchmark.

[11:03] Jordan (AE): Ok logistical items — Jordan will share POC doc and pricing, Samir will share benchmark harness and scripts, Rina will share security artifacts. Kumo will send traces. We'll schedule the benchmark window for week of Apr 21.
[11:18] Mike (Kumo): Sounds good. A couple of smaller Qs — 1) if we exceed reserved commit in production, can Redwood auto-provision more reserved capacity or is that manual? 2) Are long-running LLM caches charged differently?
[11:31] Jordan (AE): 1) Reserved capacity changes are contractual; you can add reserved pool (monthly/annual) but autoscaling uses burst pools. For production we can architect autoscaling + gradual reserved increases. 2) Cache persistence is included in runtime; there may be small storage charges for snapshotting large KV caches but it's modest — we'll specify.

[11:51] (Speaker 3): What about multi-model routing? We want to route certain flows to a higher-quality 13B overnight and 7B for daytime cheap ops.
[11:58] Samir (SE): Supported. Routing policy can be time-of-day, route-based, or SLO-based. We'll include sample routing configs.

[12:09] Aisha (Platform): For private deployment, we'll need to test KMS integration. Will Redwood use our KMS or yours?
[12:16] Rina (CSM): We support customer-managed KMS/HSM. For the POC we'll validate key exchange and encryption in transit at a high level; full key provisioning is typically done at onboarding stage.

[12:28] Lena (Product): One more product ask: provide a simple dashboard card we can embed to show current degrade %, cost burn rate, and p99 latency for stakeholders.
[12:37] Rina (CSM): We can create a custom dashboard snippet or provide APIs for you to pull the metrics.

[12:45] (Speaker 1): Ok are we missing anything?
[12:48] Jordan (AE): Quick risk list: 1) cold-start tail latency, 2) budget surprises on burst, 3) quality regressions on fallback. We'll address each with pre-warm policy, not-to-exceed budget, and canary/rollback triggers.

[13:05] Mike (Kumo): Good. If POC goes well we want a 12-month reserved commit for production with multi-region failover.
[13:11] Carlos (CTO): Agreed. Also we need enterprise contract language around data residency.
[13:16] Jordan (AE): We'll include contractual notes in the follow-up.

[13:25] Samir (SE): Technical note on metrics: we recommend capturing GPU utilization, model load time, cold-start duration, request queue depth, per-token cost, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and quality eval metrics sampled at 1% of traffic.
[13:43] Aisha (Platform): We'll aim to provide traces by Apr 15 and confirm the benchmark window by Apr 17.

[13:50] Jordan (AE): Great. Wrap up — next steps recap?
[13:54] Rina (CSM): I'll follow up with SOC2 and security docs, Jordan will send POC plan and pricing, Samir with benchmark harness. Kumo to send traces and confirm schedule.

[14:05] Mike (Kumo): Thanks everyone — excited to see results.
[14:08] (crosstalk)

End transcript.

Notes on imperfections: transcript contains a few mis-hearings ("KV cash", "kv cash") and occasional shorthand. References to amounts (like $X) left for proposal.

00:00:00 Jamie Carter: okay everyone thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time today, we packed a lot into the invite so we're gonna try to run through MSA redline status, pricing routes and then technical follow up. um Ravi and I will split, i'll cover procurement and pricing and Ravi will jump in on KMS and sandbox stuff.

00:00:18 Laura Kim: thanks Jamie, yep we wanted a short checkpoint — procurement is on a tight calendar, our finance committee meets next week so any gating docs we can get this week would help.

00:00:27 Jamie Carter: understood. quick question, Laura, do you expect the legal team to want custom language around data retention and deletion for PHI? or is standard DPA usually ok?

00:00:36 Laura Kim: short answer: we handle PHI so, yes they will want explicit deletion windows and also what happens on termination. we flagged KMS and key custody as big items too.

00:00:46 Ravi Shah: (SE) hi all, hi Laura — so on KMS we support two patterns: customer-managed keys in their cloud KMS for hosted and also bring-your-own-key to our private deployment. we treat the decryption keys never at rest in the control plane, and we can integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and Azure Key Vault. There are some HSM handoffs for on-prem but we can get you specific runbook.

00:01:12 Dr. Amir Patel: quick clarifying q — our security team insists on HSM-backed signing for audit logs, is that part of the default?

00:01:20 Ravi Shah: not in the default hosted offering — audit logs are tamper-evident and forwarded to your SIEM, but we can enable HSM-backed signing in our private deployments or as a dedicated option. it does add a bit of operational lead time, maybe 2-4 weeks to configure with the vendor's key management.

00:01:40 Laura Kim: timeline-wise that's ok if we get it documented in the MSA as a deliverable or milestone. finance wants price certainty though: can you recap pricing options, committed vs burst?

00:01:52 Jamie Carter: sure. high level we have three lanes: 1) Hosted pay-as-you-go (fastest to start, variable cost), 2) Dedicated reserved capacity (committed monthly and cheaper per token, predictable), and 3) Private (VPC/on-prem) which includes a platform fee plus support tier. For your PHI workload we usually see dedicated or private. We can structure a 12-month commit with step-down unit pricing if you sign to a reserved capacity.

00:02:20 Evan Brooks: any minimum commit? our budget team wants to avoid large upfront.

00:02:25 Jamie Carter: typical minimum is modest — we can propose a pilot commit for 3 months with an option to convert to annual. i'll send a pricing sheet with a pilot option that shows per-token economics and committed-break-even.

00:02:36 Sofia Lopez: for the SLA side, do you have a guaranteed p99 latency SLA for dedicated nodes? we need to know fallbacks in case of regional outages.

00:02:45 Ravi Shah: p99 latency SLA is available for dedicated reseller contracts; exact ms target depends on model and sequence length. we also support automated fallback to compatible model variant and cross-region failover. i'll include runbook notes on routing, and what to expect for KV cache warmup after a failover.

00:03:05 Dr. Amir Patel: our main risk is quality regressions when you fallback to a quantized variant — can you lock model versioning?

00:03:12 Jamie Carter: yes you can pin model versions and rollout policies. Redwood Optimize will also surface quality regressions by prompt set so you can catch it in early testing.

00:03:22 Laura Kim: legal asked if you will accept a limited liability carve-out for regulatory fines — we have some push back on unlimited liability.

00:03:30 Jamie Carter: fair. our standard MSA has caps tied to fees paid, but we can discuss escalation language with your counsel. i'll flag that as an item to annotate in the redline.

00:03:40 Laura Kim: great. can you share your SOC 2 report? and do you have any FedRAMP discussions?

00:03:47 Ravi Shah: we can share SOC 2 Type II report under an NDA — i'll drop the link. for FedRAMP we do not have an attestation yet; we have customers running in FedRAMP moderate paths through our private deployments but it's not a certified offering from Redwood.

00:04:05 Sofia Lopez: okay — we need to confirm with our audit team if SOC 2 is sufficient or if we'll require additional evidentiary material.

00:04:12 Jamie Carter: under stand. next let's talk about the sandbox and benchmarks — we promised a dedicated sandbox for your pilot, and a benchmark plan to validate latency and cost per token under your sequence distribution. Ravi?

00:04:22 Ravi Shah: yes. sandbox will be a dedicated pool with pinned model and KV lengths matching your workload. proposed acceptance criteria: 1) p95/p99 latency under X ms, 2) inference stability (no OOMs) for 8-hour sustained run, 3) accuracy regression below agreed delta on 500 eval prompts. We'll provide credentials and a short-runbook for KMS test keys.

00:04:50 Evan Brooks: how long to stand up the sandbox?

00:04:53 Ravi Shah: typically 3-5 business days for hosted sandbox with customer-managed KMS; if you want an isolated private deployment it can be 2-3 weeks depending on network setup and HSM provisioning.

00:05:03 Laura Kim: budget people will push back on the private option cost — is there a middle ground?

00:05:08 Jamie Carter: yes, dedicated in-cloud will hit a middle ground: predictable pricing without the full private platform fee. we can propose a 3-month dedicated pilot with commitment credit toward an annual reserved contract.

00:05:18 Dr. Amir Patel: about data residency — our regs require PHI to remain in our US region. do you support region pinning?

00:05:25 Ravi Shah: absolutely, region pinning is supported for dedicated and private. hosted API has region options but not strict residency guarantees unless on a dedicated pool in that region.

00:05:35 Laura Kim: okay that's good. legal also asked about data deletion on termination and proof of deletion.

00:05:40 Jamie Carter: we'll add deletion attestation language to the DPA. we can include a process for certified deletion and an export of logs showing deletion events.

00:05:50 Sofia Lopez: and audit logs retention?

00:05:52 Ravi Shah: default 90 days for application logs, but for dedicated/private we can extend retention and forward to your SIEM. logs are immutable once written but we can provide retention controls and signed timestamps.

00:06:10 Laura Kim: good. quick operational question: what's the escalation path if we find a production-quality regression during the pilot?

00:06:17 Jamie Carter: we'll set up a joint war room with our SEs and CSM. the MSA will include a remediation timeline and rollback policy; for pilots we do priority engineering support to remediate within X business days — we'll define exact SLA in the redline.

00:06:32 Evan Brooks: last thing — procurement wants to see a clean price sheet and an annotated MSA redline by end of week.

00:06:39 Jamie Carter: understood — i'll put the redline and pilot pricing in an email after this call.

00:06:44 Ravi Shah: i'll attach the sandbox runbook, KMS integration step-by-step, and a sample benchmark script.

00:06:50 Dr. Amir Patel: sounds good. i also want a short 30- to 60-minute bench test with our sample prompts to check model fidelity before procurement signs off.

00:06:58 Jamie Carter: we'll schedule that. aim for next Wednesday? tentative 2027-10-27?

00:07:03 Laura Kim: next Wednesday works for timing for our team.

00:07:06 Jamie Carter: perfect. any other blockers or open questions?

00:07:10 Sofia Lopez: just one — can you send the SOC 2 and the DPA redline to our security alias? names: security@pinecrest-health.com?

00:07:17 Jamie Carter: yes i'll cc that alias on the redline email.

00:07:20 Laura Kim: and also copy our procurement mailbox so it lands in the right review queue.

00:07:24 Jamie Carter: will do.

00:07:26 [mix of chatter as wrap-up]

00:07:40 Jamie Carter: OK recap: redline + pricing sheet by Jamie this week, Ravi shares KMS/runbook and sandbox playbook, customer to confirm PHI mapping and sign-off owners. we'll book the bench test for 2027-10-27. if anything changes we'll update the calendar invite.

00:08:00 Laura Kim: thank you all, this was helpful.

00:08:05 Meeting End

Notes on transcription: occasional recognition errors (HSM sometimes transcribed as "H S M"), speaker overlaps, and proper nouns may be slightly off in places. The audio was clear for most speakers but there were brief packet drop artifacts at 00:04:00.
